#79203. Latest Update: 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1535 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Trailrunnermag ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: 7 Ultrarunning Lessons Des Linden Learned from Her 100-Mile Debut

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1535 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Trailrunnermag

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred.
  • Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried.
  • Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, andy Cochrane and Nick Danielson were on the ground outside of Fountain Hills, Arizona, on October 31 to document Des Linden’s 100-mile debut at the Javelina Jundred. They bore witness to her exceptional first 60 miles, during which she took the lead in under-course-record pace, all the way through to her gritting out the remaining 40 miles to a ninth-place finish. They spoke with Linden after the race to find out what she learned—and why she’s already angling to come back.

Recent findings suggest that despite Des Linden returning to Javelina Jundred “jeadquarters” five minutes ahead of schedule and in first place, I was worried. I had followed her for the final half mile, camera rolling as her leg visibly seized up, likely from cramping. She had run 60 miles at course record pace, but still had forty to go—a long way without a fully functioning lower half. Linden sat on a chair and talked through the situation with her crew. A shoe switch, a lot more electrolytes, and roll the dice. Before I get into how the rest of her race played out, let me back up.

Being a freelance filmmaker feels a bit like being a mercenary: One moment you have no aims for the rest of the year, and the next, you’re hopping in a rental van and rallying across the Southwest during a historic October storm to get to the next job. This is exactly what my business partner Nick and I did after getting the call to document Des Linden’s first 100-mile race at the Javelina Jundred on October 31.

Sources indicate that after landing in Salt Lake City, we picked up a camper van from Roadsurfer, threw our bags in the back, and headed south on I-15. A quick stop in Moab for a 50K race of our own was followed by four days evading floods and trying to figure out which desert roads were impassable after the recent downpours—which turned out to be pretty good foretelling for the race itself.

On the three previous occasions we’ve attended this event, it has been a delightful closing chapter to the season; Javelina has served as a sort of reward for making it to the end of our race coverage for the year, where the burden of logistics is removed from the job of filming. Instead of chasing athletes across the dirt roads of the Sierra Nevada at the Western States 100 or around a heavily glaciated massif at UTMB, the athletes at Javelina run in circles back to you. Five circles, to be exact. Adding to the enjoyment factor, Javelina is typically a giant Halloween party with racers and spectators dressed in costume under the warm desert sun.

However, this year was a little different. Deluge after deluge in the 24 hours leading up to the race saturated the race course. The sky relented just before the gun went off, but by the time the race had ended, over two more inches of precipitation had fallen. Not exactly what you expect for an event in the arid Sonoran Desert outside Phoenix, Arizona, but that’s why we love ultrarunning.

Sources indicate that we did our best to keep the cameras dry and our bodies warm as we followed Linden on her third ultra—well, fourth, if you count the road 50K world record. Despite a stunning road running resume, Linden was quick to point out that she’s still a newbie at trails and ultras but is excited to keep learning. Javelina’s first three laps were nearly perfect. But soon after her body shut down it was a struggle to make it to the finish line. At one point she had to stop for almost an hour, sitting and stretching until her legs finally relaxed and let her move again. And move again she did: Linden finished her first 100-miler as the ninth woman in 16:58:01, about three hours off winner Heather Jackson. We sat down with her the day after the race to learn her biggest lessons from the process.

Linden’s biggest takeaway from Javelina is to treat 100-milers, no matter the course, weather, or circumstances, with a ton of humility. Because they ask so much of your mind and body and are a completely unique style of racing, you can’t race a 100-miler like any other distance. “Just like when I started marathons,” Linden remarked, “I learned that if you’re cavalier with how you race it, you’ll pay the price at some point.”.

Linden was patient on her first 20-mile lap, sitting a few minutes back from the leaders. Feeling good, she picked up the pace on the next two laps, picking off all of the ladies in front of her to take the lead around the halfway mark. By the time she made it to the end of the third loop at mile 60, she had a six-minute gap on second—but her legs were starting to cramp.

Industry observers note that survival quickly became the goal of lap four and the best way to do that was by listening to her pacer, Magda Boulet. Thankfully, there is no one on planet Earth better suited for the job. Boulet, a fellow U.S. Olympian in the marathon, is also a Western States winner and president of GU Energy Labs. She helped coax Linden forward, made sure she kept fueling, and stuck with her through all the ups and downs.

Industry observers note that one of Linden’s biggest challenges in the transition from road to trails and marathons to ultras is how much she needs to consume during a race—and how hard it is to catch up if she falls behind. At Javelina, Linden took most of her calories and carbs with fluids, drinking three half-liter (500 mL) bottles each lap. This fueling plan was developed for the typical heat of Javelina, but still worked well, as daytime temps almost hit 80 degrees Fahrenheit with 100% humidity.

Industry observers note that unfortunately, it wasn’t enough to keep her lower body from cramping around mile 60, which forced her to stop and stretch many times on the fourth lap. That setback resulted in her giving up the lead and ultimately the chance to win the race. “The fueling game has changed the sport,” Linden mentioned. “You see it on the roads, but especially here. It’s something I will keep working on, probably forever.”.

Industry observers note that assuming Javelina would be hot and dry like just about every other year, Linden packed for those conditions, putting her focus on cooling strategies and nutrition for the heat. She expected hardpack trails and excruciatingly hot sun, but the weather gods had other prepares. Heavy rain required Linden and her crew to scramble to find key pieces of gear, including a raincoat. And because lap four took much longer than expected, Linden ran the last couple miles of it after the sun set, sans headlamp.

It has been revealed that next time she’ll prepare for worst-case scenarios, but will also understand when to pull the plug. “You need to know when to be tough and when it’s enough,” Linden said. “If I had to do another lap, I would have been on the edge of hypothermia and the trails were so, so slippery. There is nothing wrong with saving it for another day, but also great value in staying tough.”.

Sources indicate that pacing strategy is different at every ultra, but there are some broad themes that apply to the majority of runners and racers, especially for someone with Linden’s ability to close in the back half if she’s feeling good. Surprisingly, this is similar to how she used to strategize for marathons. The first third should feel easy, the middle third is about keeping the pace steady, and the final third is when the racing begins. “The first three or even three-and-a-half laps are transportation,”  Linden said, “the final lap or two is about racing.”.

Recent findings suggest that when things got hard for Linden on the final two laps, she leaned into her crew to get to the finish. After a lap with Boulet, Linden picked up her husband Ryan as a pacer. He’s one of the most positive and energetic people you’ll ever meet, and his positivity and drive—paired with a little patience—helped get her through heavy rain and strong winds in the last 20 miles.

In a recent development, her main support at Javelina HQ was Charlie Lawrence, the 100K world record holder and good friend. “A crew that knows you well, knows the sport well, and knows the emotional ups and downs of 100 miles is a real difference maker,” Linden said. “I was excited to be around everyone all week, so it was good energy going into the race, which is key.”.

While Linden isn’t sure what the future holds or what her race calendar will look like next year, she walked away from the race with a surprising feeling. “I 100% want to come back to Javelina, it feels like unfinished business,” Linden mentioned. “I didn’t think it would be this clear, but I know I can do so much better here.”.

A Routine Invasive-Species Survey in Lake Ontario Turned Up Something Much Stranger

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.
  • Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week.
  • Sources indicate that “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Routine research in the Great Lakes system morphed into an unusual catch this fall.

In a recent development, A U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service survey crew caught a rare yellow burbot in October, according to a statement last week. The fish came from Oswego Harbor, Newly introduced York, which is on the southeastern side of Lake Ontario. It’s a significant find for more than just its color variation.

Sources indicate that “The finding is notable because burbot populations in the lake are extremely low,” the agency wrote on Nov. 10. “The species typically inhabit deeper, cooler waters than those found within the harbor.”.

Running the full length of an arm, the off-colored native burbot had xanthochromism, a genetic mutation that causes an animal’s pigment to be excessively yellow or orange. In fish, it displays on their scales and fins, but it can also show up on furred animals. It’s less common than albinism in the wild, but it’s also not unheard of.

A 6.6-foot orange-Creamsicle nurse shark turned up with the same condition, plus albinism, in 2024 in Costa Rica, and the first case of xanthochromism in a sunset-colored snook in the Gulf was documented in 2024.

According to recent reports, the variation might be appealing to fishermen, but it’s less fun for the fish themselves. Their bold coloring reduces their ability to hide within their habitat, which means they’re easy prey and often have shorter lifespans.

The deadly-bright hues look similar to banana trout, but that’s a different scenario.

It has been revealed that palomino trout, or bananas, are popular stockers for pond practice. They’re also covered in shades ranging from yellow to orange, but they’re bred that way on purpose. Hatcheries breed them from a mutant rainbow trout strain that lacks the dot pattern but keeps the bow’s notorious red lateral stripe. Despite the golden color, they aren’t related to California golden trout. The strain traces to a single yellow-mottled rainbow fingerling found at a West Virginia hatchery in 1955 and was introduced to anglers in 1963.

Read Next: These Are the Biggest North American Catfish of All Time.

As for the yellow burbot in Oswego, it wasn’t released. Its body condition was in decline, so the fish was sent to Cornell University College of Veterinary Medicine to be studied. It’s one of many fish analyzed during the region’s Aquatic Invasive Species Survey. The goal of the survey is early detection of a problem throughout the many bodies of water in the Great Lakes system, including harbors and rivers. Researchers use electrofishing, fyke nets, and gill nets to collect specimens for the survey.

#79199. The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (4073 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

The Burris Buck: How I Tagged the Biggest Mule Deer of All Time

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (4073 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me.
  • When I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Greatest Mule Deer of Them All,” appeared in the December 1975 problem of Outdoor Life. Burris’ buck remains, all these years later, the No. 1 typical mule deer buck ever taken by a hunter, according to the Boone and Crockett Club. The antlers are now owned by Cabela’s. Burris tagged the buck on Oct. 19, 1972 in Dolores County, Colorado.

I was walking the edge of a small canyon in Colorado’s San Juan National Forest when a rifle roared half a mile or so ahead of me. Till then I’d figured on stillhunting to a plateau covered with scattered oak brush 400 yards north of me. A clump of brush there would have been a fine place to take a stand.

When I heard the shot I decided to get to a vantage point on the plateau as fast as I could, so I took off at a dead run. I was almost on the plateau when I noticed movement in the oak brush and aspens on the other side of the canyon. I slammed to a stop and stared at the biggest deer I had ever seen. His body was enormous, and his rack seemed large enough for an elk.

He wasn’t running flat out, but I knew I had to shoot in a hurry. The range was about 250 yards. The buck was moving up the canyon and away from me when I found him in my Leupold 3X-to-9X scope, I put the crosshairs on his back and touched off my Sako .264. He went down in his tracks. My big-game handloads consist of 125-grain Nosler bullets backed with 66.5 grains of No. 4831 powder. It’s a very potent load.

Related: My First Buck Was the Biggest Typical Mule Deer Ever Taken with a Bow. I Almost Discarded the Antlers.

Industry observers note that I watched him for a while to make sure he wasn’t going to get up, and then I ran down a side canyon and up the other side of the big one to the fallen buck. When I ran my hands over the huge 18-point rack, I knew the antlers were very good. I was sure the deer would score high in the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book.

If someone could have told me that my 1969 Colorado buck wasn’t even good enough to make the minimum score for listing in the record book, I wouldn’t have believed him. That’s the way it turned out, but a still bigger deer was ranging the same stretch of country.

I’m 37. My wife and I live in Seguin, Texas, with our 17-year-old son and two daughters, aged 15 and eight. I’m a construction superintendent with an outfit that builds shopping centers, high-rise office buildings, and similar units.

Except for 3½ years spent in the U.S. Air Force, I’ve lived in Texas all my life. I began hunting when I was seven. My dad got me started and taught me to be a good hunter. I killed my first Texas whitetail when I was 13, and I’ve been nuts about deer hunting ever since. Though many of our Texas deer are so small we call them jackrabbits, we do have some large whitetails in the southern brush country. Some of those bucks field-dress at 200 pounds or a bit more, and some have exceptional antlers. Many years of hunting brush-country deer gave me trophy-hunting fever.

It has been revealed that I have always wanted to hunt Dall or Stone sheep in Alaska or British Columbia, but I’ve never had the money or the time. I finally decided that the next-best thing was to stay with deer and hunt trophy antlers.

My interest in camping had a lot to do with that first mule-deer hunt in Colorado in 1969. My friends and I have several four-wheel-drive vehicles and an assortment of camping gear. Charlie Fuller of Floresville, and Jack Smith of San Antonio, do a lot of hunting with me. Jack is my age. He’s a carpenter. Charlie, a few years younger, has a fertilizer-application operation. Both like to hunt deer the way I do, and they like to camp. Early in 1969 we decided to hunt in the mountains where we could camp on public land and do without guides and outfitters. We call it a “poor-boy hunt.”.

In a recent development, I did quite a bit of research on trophy mule deer before we chose the San Juan National Forest. From what I’d read in Outdoor Life and other outdoor magazines, I knew that many giant bucks were taken not too far from the Four Corners, where Utah, Arizona, Fresh Mexico, and Colorado touch.

I also bought a copy of the 1964 edition of the Boone and Crockett Club’s book, Records of North American Major Game. Study of the section on mule-deer trophies backed up my contention that southwestern Colorado would be a good place to go. We knew there were better bets, such as the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico, but we couldn’t get permits, and we wanted to go into country where we could camp on public land. We eventually drove to Cortez, Colorado, and hunted northeast of town.

The three of us all got bucks that first year, and my major buck had a rack that measured 41 inches across the outside spread. Each antler had “cheater” points extending horizontally from the outside curves of the main beams. Though the rack had a very unusual spread, the tines weren’t very long, and that’s why my trophy didn’t make the record book.

When I killed the deer, I didn’t know much about official scoring systems for massive game, but I did know that where there was one grandote (a Mexican term we use for big bucks) there should be more. We didn’t need a better reason to head back into the same area. We’ve never been sorry.

Sources indicate that the second year, I got a buck with a 33-inch outside spread. The third year, I was lucky enough to come up with another good deer. Every season I’ve hunted in those mountains, except one, I’ve taken a buck with an outside antler spread of 30 inches or better, and other members of my party have taken very good bucks too. Many hunters in the area kill deer with spreads as narrow as 12 inches. Every fall I pass up many deer to get the best one I can find.

Most of the men in our group hunt that way. We all love the mountains, and we like to hunt hard from dawn to dark. We don’t want to miss one minute of hunting on these trips. None of us will take a small buck unless time is running out on the last day.

I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too. I’m usually the cook because I enjoy it. We come into camp each evening, warm up by our wood stove in the cooktent, swap stories about what happened during the day, and take our time over meals while we strategy the next day’s hunt. Then we sack out early enough for a good rest so that we can do it all over again.

It has been revealed that we go back into the Cortez area each year because it has proved itself, and because our camping gear is suited to that kind of country. We’re not equipped to backpack into remote areas or pack in with horses.

Our cooktent, which also serves as a community area, is a 14 x 16-foot wall tent. We have 9 x 12 Coleman sleeping tents. Everybody contributes something to our outfit. We found out during our first trip that it’s best to take plenty of blankets and raingear.

Recent findings suggest that on the front end of our trailer is mounted a large box in which we pack all our food and some other items. If the weather is warm during our hunt, we have all our venison butchered, wrapped, and quick-frozen in Cortez. We pack the meat and dry ice in the box for our trip home. If the weather is cold, we hang our field-dressed deer from a game pole and then haul them home whole for butchering there. Either way, the venison we put in our freezers provides delicious meals far into the winter.

Recent findings suggest that we make our trips from Texas to Colorado with two 4WD’s. The big unit is my three-quarter-ton Dodge Power Wagon equipped with a winch. Behind the Dodge we tow a Jeep on a 20-foot trailer. We usually ride in the wagon and pack the Jeep and the trailer with gear.

Our average cost per man totals about $155, and that includes Colorado’s nonresident deer license ($50). A major chunk of the rest of each man’s expenses goes for gas. We drive straight through from Texas. That takes 20 to 24 hours, depending on driving conditions. We use the Jeep each day to put men out in hunting areas, so we burn a lot of gas. We bring plenty of steaks and a normal supply of groceries such as beans, potatoes, flour, canned goods, breakfast mixes.

Recent findings suggest that I don’t want to imply that we’re trophy crazy. Much of our pleasure derives from the planning and preparation that goes into our hunts and the talkfests that go on for months after each trip. We make the most of camp life too.

We blueprint to arrive in our hunting area the Thursday before the Saturday opener of the deer season, which is always in late October. It takes two days to set up camp, get organized, and do a little scouting. We figure on hunting three to five days, but we do not set up a hard-and-fast schedule.

As few as two men have gone to Colorado with me and as many as eight, but everything seems to go along smoothest with about four in the party. In 1972, the year I shot the world-record mule deer, there were four of us. Jack Smith went along, but Charlie Fuller couldn’t get away. Robbie Roe and Bruce Winters were my other partners. I knew them through my job, and we had done a lot of hunting together.

It has been revealed that we drove up into Colorado and camped in the same spot I’d picked out four years earlier. I knew the hunting country fairly well by that time, and I had selected five specific areas that seemed to hold the most deer and the biggest bucks. They’re all laced with relatively thick oak brush, some aspens, and a few pines. Thick oak brush is the key to success. If you’ve got tangles of that stuff and lots of them, you’re going to find deer.

The oak-brush areas most attractive to deer run to broken terrain in the form of canyons and side canyons, plateaus, and mesas. The best technique for hunting that kind of terrain is a combination of stillhunting and standing. I like to stillhunt the plateaus and small canyons. I’ve learned that deer work the small finger canyons and get down into the very bottoms of them. They range back and forth through the canyons, often go up on the mesas and plateaus.

That’s why the combination of hunting techniques works so well. When I’m stillhunting I often spot deer ahead of me or across a canyon or draw. If I take a stand on a good vantage point I may have deer working toward me.

Sources indicate that the problem is that deer may use one area today and vacate it tomorrow. So I choose an area and hunt it out. If deer are there, I stick with it; if they aren’t I move to the next area. That isn’t hard to do, because the San Juan country is mostly rolling terrain, and the altitude is only about 8,500 feet where we hunt.

Our first day of hunting in 1972 began in typical fashion. We checked the wind direction before dawn and decided on the areas each man would hunt. Then we piled into the Jeep and headed up a mountain two-track. I dropped Robbie off first and then Bruce. A few miles farther on, Jack got out of the vehicle. Dawn wasn’t much more than a dull-gray promise in the eastern sky. The black void above us was spitting drizzle.

“Robbie and Bruce will walk back to camp whenever they feel like it,” I told Jack. “You want me to pick you up at a set time, or do you want to hunt all day in the rain?”.

“I’ll meet you right here at dark,” Jack answered.

Industry observers note that I knew he’d say something like that. Jack likes to hunt as much as I do.

We all saw many deer that day, but all the bucks were small. None of us fired a shot.

Recent findings suggest that but I came very close to filling my tag on the second day of the hunt. It drizzled again, and I just ambled along till 10 o’clock. Then I got real serious about my stillhunting. I don’t know why, but the really massive bucks in that area seem to move mostly from 10 in the morning till about 1 in the afternoon.

Sources indicate that about noon I spotted a deer in thick oak brush 200 yards ahead. We were both on a plateau. The animal was a major one, so I assumed he was a buck, and I started moving in on him. My stalking was quiet because everything was wet, but I couldn’t close the distance very fast in that thick brush, and the deer kept moving away from me as he browsed.

At one point I saw part of his rack, just enough to know the antlers were in the trophy class. The excitement ended when I tried to cut him off at the edge of the plateau. When I got there, he was gone. I’ll never know whether that buck sensed my presence or went off on a predetermined course.

When Jack and I got back to camp two bucks were on the game pole. Robbie had nailed a five-pointer with his 7-mm. Remington Magnum rifle equipped with a Leupold scope. Bruce’s deer was also a five-pointer, but the antlers were heavier. Bruce collected his venison with a Winchester Model 70 .30/06 rigged with a Leupold scope.

Industry observers note that when we awoke the third morning, the dad-gummed drizzle was still with us. I suited up in my Browning raingear and filled my pockets with dried fruits and jerky. I knew it would be another long day before I could bake myself beside the wood stove in the cooktent. I dropped Jack off on the trail and then drove on and parked near the area I had hunted the day before.

Industry observers note that A slight breeze was coming down off the mountain, so I decided to stillhunt into it and get farther back into rougher country. About 9 o’clock I started into a 400-yard-wide canyon and began working up toward one rim. I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

Industry observers note that then I looked at them through my Bausch & Lomb 7 x 35 binoculars. Both were definitely in the trophy class. It was fairly late in our hunt, so I decided it was best to cash in on one of them. I’d make the stalk and decide which rack was best when I got within range.

It has been revealed that I was about three-quarters of the way to the top when I spotted two bucks feeding in a clearing 1,000 yards away in the canyon. I stopped and watched them for several minutes because I was astonished that I could see their racks from such a great distance with the naked eye.

I eased on through the oak brush for about 200 yards and busted out a doe. She pushed on ahead of me. I didn’t think she would spook the bucks, but I watched them for several minutes to make sure. They continued feeding away from me up the slope. I could keep them in sight at this point because they were still in a clearing.

It has been revealed that I eased back into some cover and stalked ahead for about 45 minutes while the drizzle came on stronger and stronger. During that time I didn’t see the bucks, because they had moved into a patch of brush, but I was pretty sure they were still nearby. I would have seen them if they had moved out on that slope. There was a 75-yard-wide opening at the top of the canyon, and I would have seen or heard them if they had run back toward me or along the canyon bottom.

An additional 30 minutes passed before I decided I couldn’t be more than 200 yards from the deer, but I still couldn’t see them — the patch of brush was up to 10 feet tall. Then I busted out a doe again. She crashed along toward the bucks. I figured they’d spook, so I took off at a dead run for an opening 20 yards ahead of me. If I was going to do any good, I had to shoot in a hurry.

In a recent development, just as I broke into the opening, three deer ran into view. Two were the bucks I’d been stalking; the third was still bigger. He was lagging behind, and even in the split-second I had to shoot, I knew he had the best rack by far.

It has been revealed that my handloaded Nosler 125-grain bullet flew 300 yards, ripped into the buck’s heart-lung area, and blew up. He stumbled, hit the ground, and lay still.

When I examined the antlers — six unbelievably massive tines on the right side and five on the left — I knew I had killed the finest trophy buck I’d ever seen, but I had no idea that he was the best typical mule deer ever taken. The enormous body of the deer concerned me most at the moment.

According to recent reports, normally we can drive a vehicle close to our kills and then drag the deer out to the 4WD. But I was way back in rough country, and we couldn’t approach with a vehicle. It would have been impossible for me to drag that deer very far by myself.

Sources indicate that I decided to hike out to the Jeep and drive back to camp for help. Since Robbie and Bruce had already killed their bucks, the odds were they would be in camp. They were. We went back to my deer, dressed and quartered it, and packed the quarters and the head out to the vehicle. When we returned to camp we found Jack waiting for us. He needed some help with a heavy-antlered five-pointer he’d killed with his .270 Weatherby Magnum. By the time we got that buck out, the day and the hunt were finished.

When I got home I took my buck’s head and cape to taxidermist Ed Schlier in San Antonio for mounting. He’s an official measurer for the Boone and Crockett Club, so we rough-scored the green antlers. Our preliminary figures indicated my buck would be among the top 10 listed in the typical-mule-deer category. That was exhilarating, but I didn’t think much more about it till one night several months later when my phone rang at 1 a.m.

Recent findings suggest that “Doug,” Ed blurted out, “I think your buck may be the best typical mule deer ever taken. I scored the antlers this evening, and I couldn’t believe it when I came up with a total score of two-hundred twenty-six! That’s nine better than the previous world-record typical mule deer. I’ve been double-checking my figures for hours, but they always come out the same. If they hold up with Boone and Crockett officials, you’ve got a fresh world record. I figured that news was worth waking you up.”.

It sure was, but it was just the beginning.

Sources indicate that the North American Big Game Award Program — jointly sponsored by the Boone and Crockett Club and the National Rifle Association — requires that any big-game trophy likely to win an award must be rescored by a panel of judges. Accordingly, I sent the mounted head off to the program headquarters in Washington, DC.

In February 1974 the program coordinator phoned me and invited me to attend the Fifteenth North American Substantial Game Awards meeting on March 24 in Atlanta, Georgia. I guessed my buck had proven good enough to win some kind of award, but I was too busy to go to Atlanta.

That was my position till I received several more calls from other program officials. They told me that if I missed the awards meeting, I would very much regret it later, so I scraped together some cash, cancelled several appointments, and flew to Atlanta.

In a recent development, at the banquet I was presented with the award for the best typical mule deer taken during the most recent three-year award period. I also received official recognition for taking a latest world record. In addition I won the Sagamore Hill Award, which is given only to hunters whose outstanding trophies are of great distinction. This award is the highest given by the Boone and Crockett Club. Only one may be given during any big-game-award period, and only 10 have been presented during the club’s history.

I was stunned. When I think about it, even today, I’m still stunned.

Former shooting editor Jim Carmichel wrote a short sidebar about his predictions for the next record-book mule deer.

Bagging a trophy mule deer hinges on four key factors: 1) luck, 2) hunting skill, 3) a firm determination to pass up lesser deer, 4) a carefully conducted survey of the areas likely to produce significant mule-deer bucks at a predetermined point in time. The last three are more or less under the control of the hunter, but the fourth requires a basic understanding of trophy development.

A look at the Boone and Crockett Club’s record book highlights that a large percentage of trophy mule deer have consistently been taken from certain fairly well-defined regions. Equally significant is that the trophy heads from these regions have been taken within specific time periods. During the early 1960’s, for example, a good number of high-ranking bucks were taken at the Jicarilla Apache Reservation in New Mexico. It’s no secret that certain areas tend to provide the natural requirements (such as a rich mineral diet) necessary for the development of big antlers, and that certain genetic strains of deer tend to produce big racks. Arizona’s Kaibab area, to give but one example, is one of the regions well known for its ability to grow large-antlered mule deer. However, this doesn’t mean that these areas always abound with record-busting bucks. This is where the vital time element enters the picture.

Read Next: The Story of the Allison Buck, and the Best Opening Morning in Ohio History.

If a big-buck-producing area is allowed to rest for a few seasons, with little or no hunting pressure, the bucks grow old and develop larger and larger antlers. Then word gets around about all the big bucks to be found there, and hunting pressure increases. In three or four years all the big trophy bucks have been killed off. When trophies become hard to find, the hunting pressure drops off, and the cycle begins again.

Industry observers note that the smart trophy hunter keeps track of the best areas and keeps a discerning eye on the hunting pressure in these places. The idea, of course, is to get there a season or two ahead of the crowd.

According to recent reports, legs shortened on the tripod shooting sticks, rifle secure in the saddle, I eased the setup onto a small rise in front of me. As I crawled into position, a buck materialized in the scope. It had no idea I was there.

Recent findings suggest that A quick range reading followed by another confirmed the distance, 236 yards. The evening air was dead calm.

Industry observers note that when I twisted the scope’s throw lever to 18X, the whitetail filled the field of view. The shot was simple: one bullet from a Browning 6.8 Western dropped the deer, and my 2026 season was off to a good start.

Industry observers note that from the oak-studded knob on which I shot, I could see the North Umpqua River meandering through the valley below. It was on this river that I caught my first summer steelhead, at age 4, in 1968. In 1986 I shot my first wild turkey from the same area. That hunt sparked a 40-year passion chasing these grand birds.

Sources indicate that as I walked up on the high-racked buck, the river’s unique beauty was captivating. I wasn’t looking at just any whitetail, but a prized Columbia whitetail. Here we have the only huntable population of these special deer in the world. I was exactly one hour and 20 minutes from my home in Western Oregon.

According to recent reports, almost 50 years to the day prior, I shot my very first deer — a Columbia blacktail. That buck came less than 15 miles from my home. Over the decades I’ve shot some dandy blacktails and seen bigger ones that outsmarted me. I rank consistently killing a mature trophy Columbia blacktail as the most challenging of all substantial game hunting in North America. The habitat they call home is vast, varied and as dense as a tropical rainforest in places.

Less than a week after punching the whitetail tag I was in Oregon’s Coast Range. I saw seven bears in four days before shooting a mature, sleek-coated beauty. My wife and I love bear meat; she even renders the fat for cooking. It’s great this time of year.

In the spring I hunted bears in the same area of the Coast Range. I passed 27 bears in seven days before pulling the trigger on a nice bruin.

Earlier this month, friends and I got serious about duck hunting public land on nearby rivers, as we always do this time of year. The first two hunts found us targeting wood ducks. I shot seven-bird limits of the gorgeous little ducks each time out. The following trip was a mix of mallards and woodies, and after that, an all-mallard limit. Excellent eating, all of them.

One morning was extra special, as I achieved something I’d been trying to pull off for three seasons. The morning was foggy and wood ducks aggressively poured into the small spread of decoys. Shots were close. I took seven wood ducks along with a pair of honkers. While driving home with the double limit I got a text from a nearby landowner. A major flock of turkeys was back on his property. He asked if I’d come shoot some, as they were becoming a nuisance.

In recent years Oregon created a special hunt for problematic fall and winter turkeys. It’s called a beardless turkey permit and with it you can shoot three turkeys without visible beards, on each of the three available permits that are purchased over the counter. It’s a depredation hunt that was put in place to deter large flocks of fall turkeys from congregating on private property, causing damage and leaving messy gifts that are a health concern to pets and livestock. Since funding to trap and relocate turkeys was cut in the state, turkey numbers have exploded in many counties. It’s common to see multiple flocks a day of 100 or more turkeys, all fall and winter long, in several places around Oregon.

I hurried home, grabbed Echo, my pudelpointer, and headed out for the turkeys. Echo is almost 13 years old. She’s hunted fall turkeys every year of her life. Oregon is one of a handful of Western states that allows the use of dogs for fall turkey hunting. It’s one of my favorite hunts of the year and Echo loves it. For Kona, my 10-year-old male pudelpointer who I lost to an intestinal torsion this past September, this was his favorite hunt of all. It was hard heading afield without him, for the first time.

In a recent development, but Echo didn’t skip a beat. After some searching we finally located the flock of turkeys. There were 46 of them, all hens, jakes, and jennies. They fed on the edge of a grassy meadow, heading uphill toward a patch of Douglas fir timber. When the time was right, I sent Echo. She ran at the flock as fast as her aging legs could carry her. She’d done this many times in her life. She knew the drill. If all the birds flushed, I’d call her back, we’d sneak into the timber, set up and call the flock back in. That didn’t happen.

This time Echo caught the turkeys by surprise. A few flew into the trees but most burrowed into thick blackberries and tall, green ferns. Echo struck the perfect point and held it until I arrived. Turkeys often hold tight as quail. When I got to Echo, a jake made a run for it. It didn’t make it far. At the shot, the rest of the flock scurried, some running, some taking wing. I shot another bird on the run, then dropped one more from the air. Echo couldn’t gather them fast enough. Finally, my bird trifecta was completed.

We ate birds for dinner that night, and Tiffany whipped up multiple dishes for a significant church potluck the following day. Everyone enjoyed the local bounty, and there was an extra sense of pride among the elderly men who used to hunt.

In a recent development, I’ve been fortunate to hunt much of the country, and even lived in Alaska for a stint in the 1990s. When it comes to hunting and fishing, I’ve found no other state that matches what Oregon has to offer. It boasts hunting opportunities for 12 massive game species, including four subspecies of deer. It has the best turkey hunting I’ve seen, with 14 tags available a year, including three spring toms. Thirty-three of the 41 recognized waterfowl species can be hunted here, along with bonus Eurasian wigeon which are becoming more frequent. Wigeon are my favorite duck to hunt and they thrive in the valleys and coast.

Sources indicate that if you’re into predator hunting, coyotes and bobcats abound statewide. Mountain lions are now classified as big game in Oregon. In the past few years I’ve called in eight cougars, shooting the last one at 12 paces, using a shotgun. Last year I caught 11 different lions on trail cameras in one morning, all within 25 miles of my home–seven were within two miles. Cougars are thick, I wish we could hunt them with hounds as numbers are out of control. But some of our game laws make zero sense.

Recent findings suggest that most recently Oregon made national news for the infamous Oregon Initiative Petition 28. IP 28 didn’t even appear on the November ’26 ballot. Yet, just about every blurb on the topic for the past year made it appear certain Oregon was going to lose all hunting and fishing privileges. Much of the press and pursuers of clickbait chastised Oregonians, ignorant of the full story and who the players were. In the fine print, IP 28 was absurd not only to hunters and anglers, but cattle ranchers, farmers, pet owners and more folks in our state.

Industry observers note that I was stunned at the number of fellow outdoorsmen who threw Oregon sportsmen under the bus, telling them to move from the state. Oregon is not the problem. Our issue is that the state is largely governed by people in three cities. The hunting and fishing population outside those city limits is large, and the many animals thriving in the game-rich state know no such boundaries nor are they aware of the people who set the rules. One hunting or fishing trip to our great state will reveal how special it truly is.

Sources indicate that for the past 26 years I’ve made a living as a full-time writer and wildlife photographer. For 14 of those years I hosted hunting and fishing TV shows. I’ve written more than 4,200 magazine articles and 17 books with more in the works. I couldn’t have done it if not for living in Western Oregon, in the little town of Walterville — named after people on my wife’s side of the family.

According to recent reports, minutes from my home there’s something to hunt or fish for every day of the year. I live on the McKenzie River, a tributary of the famed Willamette River. I caught my first spring chinook salmon from the McKenzie in the 1960s. Over the decades, it, along with the Willamette River, have produced thousands of springers and loads of summer steelhead and rainbow trout for my family. Growing up fishing these rivers  spoiled me.

The Willamette River is major, wide, and challenging to fish in places. Downstream from where the Willamette flows into the mighty Columbia River, you’ll find some of the world’s best salmon and sturgeon fishing.

The McKenzie River is a blue ribbon rated trout stream, one of the best in the country. Growing up, word traveled fast when movie stars were on the water, most presenting dry flies to try and entice stunning redsides.

Sources indicate that A few miles from my home, Theodore Roosevelt loved to fish for rainbow trout. I know where he stayed and the holes he liked to fish. Rumor has it–from some of my wife’s relatives who homesteaded the McKenzie River Valley in the mid-1800s–it was among Roosevelt’s favorite rivers to fish, both for the trout and the sheer beauty the region offered. Roosevelt would be happy to know that the place he so loved is now teeming with wildlife, including elk that carry his name.

It has been revealed that in fourth grade I began trapping. My parents took turns taking me to check traps before school. For sets close to home, I’d ride my bike. Beaver, raccoon, coyote, red fox and bobcat were some of the target species. I skinned the catch after school. This continued into my freshman year of high school, until sports consumed my life. Trapping greatly educated me about the land and the animals that live there. It also allowed me to make some money so I could fish in the summer months, rather than work.

In the 1970s, most duck hunting I experienced was on the rivers. In my formative years Dad, Grandpa and I spent many days together in duck and goose blinds.

According to recent reports, less than an hour from my home the first ring-necked pheasants were introduced to the continental United States. Birds arrived by sea in 1882, from China. Dad and grandpa shared many stories of incredible pheasant hunts they had in the 1950s and ‘60s. “Best pheasant hunting in the country,” Grandpa said. He wasn’t wrong. Today, we don’t pester what few pheasants remain in the valley. But parts of Eastern Oregon are flourishing with ring-necks. A few years back, Echo and I secured a limit of ducks, pheasants and valley quail on one of our best days, ever.

Industry observers note that valley quail and mountain quail thrive around my home. Getting on multiple coveys a day is common. The occasional ruffed grouse is put up in the valley, but they’re more prevalent in the foothills of the Cascades and Coast Range. Just above ruffed grouse in the mountains are blue grouse. When I was a kid we never saw a blue grouse below 2,000 feet. Today we shoot a lot of the major birds at and below 500 feet. More than once I’ve taken valley and mountain quail, blue and ruffed grouse on the same day. Truly special hunts, all of them.

In mid-September band-tailed pigeons are the target. They occupy both mountain ranges and parts of the valley floor. In my days of youth the daily limit was seven, today it’s only two. Still, dogs love these hunts, as does my 86-year-old father. Intercepting speeding birds as they fly ridgelines in search of berries, minerals and water makes for challenging shooting and steep country retrieves.

Sources indicate that in the fall we chase Western gray squirrels. Kona loved treeing gray squirrels almost as much as he reveled in fall turkey hunting. The furry tree-dwellers are delicious.

For decades, cackling Canada geese have flocked to the Willamette Valley to graze on rye grass. The Willamette Valley is dubbed The Grass Seed Capital Of The World, and this prime food attracts loads of big game and waterfowl. Minimas — the smallest of the cackling Canada geese — regularly funnel into big decoy spreads in flocks of 10,000 or more. Words can’t be heard over the screaming little geese.

Industry observers note that thirty minutes from home, in multiple directions, is the best duck hunting I’ve found anywhere in the country. One day you’re hunting wigeon and pintails in flooded fields; the next, picking greenheads in tiny creeks surrounded by tall trees. You can regularly shoot a seven drake limit of wood ducks on public waters and private land filbert orchards, what outsiders call hazelnuts. The valleys hold some of the world’s best soil for filbert farming. As these orchards have expanded in recent years, wood duck and mallard numbers continue to grow because they love feasting on the nuts. Today there are more wood ducks than I ever recall seeing in my 51 years of hunting them.

According to recent reports, as I finalize these words, I’m preparing for the next several days afield, all near home. Tomorrow I’ll be hunting wood ducks on the river. The day after that, checking my 75 trail cameras set in the nearby hills. And the day after that I head to the Coast Range to hunt secretive Roosevelt elk in the rainforest. Last November I took a 340-class Roosevelt 35 minutes from home, my biggest Roosy bull to date.

In a recent development, there’s no better place to be, doing what I love the most. Oregon is a grand place to grow up, and to grow old.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov.
  • It has been revealed that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The seven-person panel that constitutes Idaho’s Fish and Game Commission is down to six after commissioner Brody Harshbarger resigned Wednesday amid pressure from sportsmen and at least one state lawmaker. Harshbarger took a plea deal on Nov. 9 to dismiss five of seven charges related to illegally killing two bull elk in the region he represents.

Recent findings suggest that “Your service on the commission is concluded, effective immediately,” wrote Gov. Brad Little’s chief of staff, Zach Hauge, in response to Harshbarger’s resignation, obtained by the Idaho Capital Sun. “Maintaining the integrity, credibility and effective operation of the Idaho Fish and Game Commission remains a top priority for Gov. Little.”.

It has been revealed that harshbarger was charged in March with seven wildlife violations from the 2025 hunting season, including poaching two bull elk in Fremont County, where he lives. The former commissioner stepped away from commission duties once he was charged, but retained his seat until this week while the case continued, effectively leaving the position vacant.

Related: Idaho Wildlife Commissioner Charged with Poaching Elk, Trespassing, Says He’ll ‘Voluntarily Postpone’ Duties.

“I understand everyone deserves their day in court, but commissioners are charged with making and upholding our regulations,” Nick Fasciano, executive director of the Idaho Wildlife Federation, tells Outdoor Life. “And we do expect them to be held to a higher standard. The whole thing is disappointing.”.

Recent findings suggest that the commission sets statewide hunting, fishing, and trapping seasons plus bag limits and other regulations based on recommendations and research supplied by Idaho Department of Fish and Game scientists. Each member of the commission can serve two four-year terms, and no more than four commissioners can come from the same political party. Harshbarger is a farmer in Ashton, Idaho. It’s an area known for massive chunks of public land and substantial grain and potato operations.

“I love our wildlife and the community we live in,” Harshbarger’s profile read on the commission’s website before it was removed. “We have a lot of challenges, and I am excited to help continue to solve them. What an amazing place to live and work.”.

Harshbarger pled guilty to hunting without a tag and shooting across a road. The remaining five charges, which are being dismissed in exchange for his guilty plea, are two illegal big-game kills, hunting from a vehicle, failure to retrieve game, and trespass (one bull was on private property).

Industry observers note that when news of Harshbarger’s plea deal went public, hunters and anglers started contacting regional IDFG offices and the governor’s office to demand his removal. The plea deal means his penalties could be as low as $500 and a one-year hunting suspension when he’s sentenced Dec. 9.

Frustration has also boiled over on social media around Harshbarger’s case.

Recent findings suggest that “Wake up Governor Little and do the right thing,” one Instagram user commented on the news of the plea deal, prior to Harshbarger’s resignation. “You and Senator Risch are already working to sell off our public lands and now you won’t step in to protect our wild game. Shame on you two.”.

Industry observers note that harshbarger was appointed by Gov. Little in 2024.

Recent findings suggest that “Public trust is difficult to earn and easily lost,” wrote Idaho state Rep. David Leavitt in an email sent to Little on Tuesday that called for Harshbarger’s dismissal. “Maintaining that trust requires us to uphold the same principles regardless of who is involved. Idaho citizens deserve nothing less.”.

According to recent reports, little is also now in charge of appointing the director of IDFG. The commission did that until this year, when Little signed a publicly opposed bill into law changing the procedure from a seven-person decision to a one-person appointment by the governor, with confirmation by the state Senate.

“Commissioners and the director now serve at the pleasure of the governor,” Fasciano indicates. “The commission is not empowered to boot out one of their own members even if they were so inclined.”.

Current IDFG director Jim Fredericks, a career fisheries biologist, was already leading the agency when the new law took effect July 1, making him the state’s last director selected by the commission.

Read Next: Montana Man Banned from Hunting for 20 Years After Bowhunters Watch Him Poach a Trophy Bull.

Recent findings suggest that “The actual department of Fish and Game is going to take some heat for this [Harshbarger incident], but they weren’t the decision makers here,” Fasciano indicates. “The commission and the director were not able to drive a resolution here and they are also not responsible for the sentencing. A lot of frustration is going to be directed toward them, that isn’t their fault.”.

Tech Report: Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship.
  • After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not.
  • Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

Industry observers note that this interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

According to recent reports, I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

Recent findings suggest that I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

Industry observers note that and then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

Sources indicate that and then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

According to recent reports, and so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a major thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

In a recent development, I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

In a recent development, I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

It has been revealed that now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

Sources indicate that I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Stalking Deer Like a Real Woodsman

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the massive whitetail buck and I badly startled each other.
  • After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding.
  • Recent findings suggest that but then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the massive whitetail buck and I badly startled each other. In the steady rain patter, he apparently didn’t hear me until I’d stillhunted very close to his cedar clump shelter. I almost came unglued when he exploded into view, too spooked to even snort.

After the rifle’s roar shattered the forest stillness, I heard a couple more rhythmic thumps as the by-now invisible deer continued bounding. So much for my semi-frantic snapshot.

Recent findings suggest that but then came a distant, wood-splintering racket, followed by silence. Without snow, it took awhile to slowly, alertly follow up. I found the heart-shot buck. That terminal crash noise came from his failing to clear a windfall when the carburetor quit for keeps.

That’s stillhunting at its best. Unlike the prolonged tedium of trail watching or waiting out a drive, stillhunting’s uptight anticipation is an ongoing thrill. When the action does come, it’s often sudden, without warning. Don’t hunt this way if you have a weak heart.

Industry observers note that very old-timers like my 87-year-old father tell me that forest stillhunting was far more common decades ago. Maybe today’s urban hunters don’t trust their stealth and woodcraft skills. Although not an easy way to take woodland game, including elk, the bottom-line reality is that stillhunting can produce game when other tactics cannot.

Obviously, a lone-wolf hunter can’t make drives to himself. Even when sufficient manpower is available, effective drives require thorough knowledge of both the terrain and how local deer use it. If game chooses not to move because it fed well last night, lacks sexual ambition just now or doesn’t like the prevailing weather, trail watching is usually hopeless. For that matter, many mule deer and most elk and moose simply don’t stick that much to established trails.

The stillhunter is free of such vagaries. Instead of hoping game will come to him, he goes to it — although stillhunting is not the stalking of game already located. Tactically, he has two top priorities. First, to move quietly and alertly, his course basically dictated by wind, terrain and possibly sun direction. Second, to discover game before it sees, hears or smells him. The stillhunter must play a lone-hand game — two hunters seem to make not twice, but four times the noise of one hunter.

Slow movement is a must. A stillhunter covering ground too swiftly simply can’t look well enough for concealed game. He also can’t help making extra noise to be picked up by critters who depend on acute hearing every day of their lives to stay out of trouble. They easily detect high frequency noises (including any rustles, squeaks or metallic clinks from our gear and garb) that we often can’t hear.

Industry observers note that the real trick in stillhunting is to do the looking and the moving as two separate functions. If you forget everything else, remember that! When you attempt to look for game and move your feet at the same time, sooner or later you will make unwanted noise — snapping a brittle twig, tripping noisily or whatever.

Sources indicate that don’t follow any set rhythm of taking a set number of steps, then stopping. Instead, consider the area that you can see from where you stand as one vision zone. I never move until this zone, of up to 180° ahead and to both sides, has been totally studied.

Recent findings suggest that A vision zone may range out only 50 feet in dense woods or 200-plus yards in more open country. Depending on the extent of the zone, terrain and cover, it may take 30 seconds or several minutes of methodical looking. Often a promising area is worth the time to just sit for extra eyeballing.

Don’t expect to see a full-blown deer or elk looming up ahead like calendar artwork. Look for just parts of the animal as clues. Most forest visuals are vertical lines — tree trunks, etc. An out-of-place horizontal line may be a log or the outline of a deer’s back. A smudge of dull yellow may be autumn leaves or an elk rump. Wide-field binoculars help greatly on such details.

In a recent development, once, while hunting in the Cascade Mountains, my eye caught a tiny movement ahead. A broad leaf twitching with the breeze? But there was no breeze and, in that evergreen thicket, no deciduous leaves. I waited some minutes, then spotted the movement again for what it was — a blacktail doe’s ear twitching as its owner listened. When she finally moved, right behind her came a shootable buck.

Industry observers note that after searching a visual zone (and listening, too), select a route for the next few feet or yards, based on avoidance of brush contact or other potential noise. Footwork is vital. Short steps are quietest. They offer best control of shifting your balance if you ease your foot down and feel a twig likely to snap under full weight. Also, only with short steps can you come down slowly and silently on your toes or the ball of your foot. Long steps force the heel down first, making it much more likely that you will snap twigs or make a soft but tell-tale thud.

Want some expert stillhunting lessons? Simply watch a house cat on the prowl for birds or field mice. Slow movement, long look-listen pauses, obvious patience and great concentration are what make felines the finest stillhunters in nature. Once, in Washington’s mountains, I watched a mountain lion on the prowl. This best-of-all deer hunter resembles a magnified house cat at work.

Big or small, hunting cats are superb at using concealment. You should do likewise. Very often, unseen game ahead will hear you. By moving slowly with minimum noise, you may sound much like just another deer. But the listening quarry will be watching in your direction for visual confirmation. Don’t slow yourself any more than necessary. I use camouflage makeup to make my pale face less visible against dark forest backdrop.

In a recent development, if you can move quietly in some kind of concealment, use that route rather than an easier-looking, more open course. Stick to shadows; avoid sunlit patches. When possible, hunt with the sun behind you. Go over ridgetops with caution, using brush or timber cover. If the hilltop lacks cover, try crawling. Of course, stillhunting must be done into the wind or at least across it — never downwind. Although human sense of smell is pretty pathetic, sometimes the barnyard odor of elk ahead can be detected.

Often a stillhunter has the option of following fresh game tracks. Except under ideal conditions, such as new snow, one-man tracking demands so much attention that the stillhunter is distracted while he should be looking for actual game. More than once, deer or elk have surprised me, costing me a shot simply because I was distracted by some interesting tracks. If you start trailing, remember that the maker of these tracks may be bedded down somewhere ahead and almost certainly watching his backtrail. To get anywhere close to it will require extremely good stillhunting.

The lay of the land can be friend or foe. Ridges and hills offer chances to surprise game on the other side. Flat country is tougher because it offers few elevation advantages to the hunter. Although knowing the area always helps, it’s not truly essential for stillhunting. Once, a young stillhunter in our party, new to the place, nailed a whitetail buck the second morning. A fast learner, he capped that next year by pussyfooting close enough to a Cascades bull elk to take him with a bow.

The inexperienced stillhunter is often tempted to work mature evergreen timber, where dense shade means little underbrush. But closely spaced conifers self-prune their branches profusely, forming a noisy layer of dead twigs. Such forests can be hunted only when there’s enough wind noise to cover the hunter’s snap-crackle-pop progress. Unless soggy from rain or wet snow, dead leaves are another audio booby trap.

Sources indicate that some timber is open enough to have a good growth of clover or grass, particularly attractive to elk. By contrast, dense coniferous forests contain little ground-level browse to attract feeding game, but they often provide good escape cover when hunting pressure is on. In unseasonably warm weather, the cool shade of thick evergreen timber invites game. In cold weather, the evergreen canopy traps radiant ground heat for considerably warmer bedding than more open forests.

Sources indicate that where evergreen timber is lacking, game makes the best of thick brushy cover or tall grasses — the latter is commonly a deer favorite. In real cold or after rain, any warming sun draws game to south or west-facing slopes.

It has been revealed that best time of day for stillhunting depends on several factors. Stillhunting as early as light permits may find game feeding or on the move to bedding. Ground litter then is less noisy, thanks to the night’s dampening dew. But if overnight frost has made fallen leaves ultra-brittle or has crusted the snow, better wait for some midday thawing.

Industry observers note that though rain or a moderate wind helps mask hunter movement sounds, strong winds are a mixed blessing. With their hearing impaired by too much wind, restless animals change location often rather than staying put. That aids the stillhunter, because moving game is far easier to see. But wind-jittery animals, up on their feet and watching for danger they can’t hear, can spot the hunter more readily. Fortunately, a stiff wind covers his extra noise if the stillhunter sticks to thicker cover for extra concealment.

According to recent reports, worst of all are those dead-calm Indian summer days, when even your shadow seems to make a racket in the dried-out forest. The only option, then, is to hunt terrain where game can be spotted at a considerable distance (example: from one ridge to another).

Some cover simply can’t be stillhunted. Swampy terrain is impossibly noisy, all the more if there’s any ice to be broken. Dry, fluffy snow can be fairly quiet for walking. But typical autumn snow, heavy and wet, is composed of oversize, many-pointed flakes. Each step compression-shatters untold thousands of such crystalline flakes. That accounts for the appallingly loud squeakiness. Until it’s settled, breaking its flakes in the process, such snow is no good for stillhunting. The settling process may take two or three days unless a thaw speeds it.

Snow characteristics may vary with terrain. North-facing snow is little affected by the weak sun of late autumn, but snow on southern and western slopes settles quickly with a few hours of sun.

According to recent reports, the stillhunter must remember that weather affects game’s likely location. The first serious snowfall often causes deer to hole up in the shelter of thick, low-branching evergreens, where they may stay 48 to 72 hours, believe it or not, even during the rut. Hungry when they finally leave cover, deer then are likely to feed during the day. But until they start moving, the pristine snow will be barren of tracks, leading to the false conclusion that all game has moved out.

In a recent development, of course, game does move out of high country when major snowstorms hit. Hunting deer and elk on such vertical migration routes is often considered a trail-watching game. The stillhunter can cover more territory to learn where game is moving — and if it’s moving.

It has been revealed that gear and clothing are critical in stillhunting. Soft leather boots with crepe soles are almost moccasin-quiet but treacherous in steep, wet or rocky terrain. Classic, Maine-style, rubber shoepacs make quiet steps. Their rounded sole edges are not as likely to shear-snap noisy twigs as stiffer, sharp-edged soles do. With any other rubber footwear, wear enough socks to prevent empty space around the foot from audibly pumping air at each step.

It has been revealed that harder, composition soles with lugs are necessary to maintain life and limb in rough country. Alas, such footwear is noisier. The only consolation is that in country steep enough to require lug-soled boots, the stillhunter has a longer “working range” across canyons, etc., and is not quite as vulnerable to making noise as the close-range, flatland hunter. At times, I’ve carried soft sneakers in my daypack to slip on after climbing a ridge that demanded lug-soled, ankle-supportive boots. Another useful trick is to wear a pair of knit leg warmers running from knee-height to ankles. These muffle twig noise and grass swish.

In a recent development, clothing choice is very simple. Whatever the material, it must be soft. Nylon, corduroy and stiff denim are too noisy. Wool and flannel are the great favorites for quiet movement. Some synthetics like orlon and acrylic are almost as good, depending on weave and nap. Rubberized raingear makes less noise than nylon or vinyl. Because a hat’s brim snags noisy branches, wear a cap. Again, wool or knitted acrylic is quietest. I made a simple, woolen pack cover to keep my backpack from imitating a snare drum when I hunker through overhanging branches.

For quiet carrying, a firearm’s barrel length is more critical than weight per se. Although carbines are best, one of my favorite woods rifles has a 24-inch barrel. I find a 26-inch barrel is just too easy to bang against branches. A timber riflescope should have at least a 30-foot field at 100 yards — more would be better, because forest shots are often at close-range game on the run. Yellow shooting glasses contrast brown deer and elk better against evergreen backgrounds.

Pocket hardware like keys, coins and cartridges must be handkerchief-wrapped to eliminate tell-tale clinking. When I rendezvoused with my deer-hunting daughter in the woods, her sardonic greeting was, “Hello, Santa!”.

In a recent development, “Well before I saw you,” she continued, “I could hear you playing ‘Jingle Bells’. What’s in your pockets?”.

Industry observers note that A ring of unwrapped keys, that’s what. And deer probably could hear it twice as well as she could.

Although usually not physically taxing, stillhunting is tiring if you do it right. What wears you out is the strain of constant vigilance. And I mean constant! About the time you relax or daydream, up bounds a buck or bull that makes good his escape because you weren’t mentally prepared to react quite fast enough. But if you’re a dedicated hunter, the high-tension hours of stillhunting are memorable whether you score or not.

It has been revealed that this story, “Deer on the Prowl,” appeared in the January 1990 problem of Outdoor Life. Read more from this series:.
