#79191. The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Skimag ↗ Open Full Page

The Most Unexpected Ski Adventure in North America Might Be in Michigan

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Skimag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe.
  • “Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head.
  • It has been revealed that the Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Marcus Caston, Mt. Bohemia, Mich. (Photo: Keri Bascetta).

It’s breakfast in the main yurt, so the girl from the kitchen is again standing on a chair and rubbing the dome of a snow globe. Eyes shut tight, she shouts over the gathered skiers.

“Grant us snow, almighty spirits of winter,” she begins, raising the globe above her head. “By your power, give us powder. Amen.” She is our shaman.

“Amen,” we all murmur along and mean it.

It has been revealed that the Midwest is a peculiar place for a ski pilgrimage. But on Michigan’s isolated Keweenaw Peninsula, known as “the fin,” Mount Bohemia has no shortage of true believers. And they’re not coming for the corduroy. This expert-only backcountry resort is ungroomed, technical, and seriously steep. Signs across the mountain are clear: NO BEGINNERS ALLOWED.

While skiers scour the globe for powder, Michigan has been sitting on one of the country’s most unlikely stashes. Bohemia sees almost 300 inches annually, with no snowmaking. Here, bad weather is usually good news. Arctic air sweeping over Lake Superior’s warmer water produces storms that bury the Keweenaw. This lake-effect snow is remarkably light and dry—the kind you’d travel to Utah or Japan to find.

On paper, Bohemia’s numbers seem modest: 900 vertical feet, 585 acres, and just two lifts. Yet over 90 percent of its runs are black diamond or better, including the region’s only triple-blacks. Boho has the untamed feel of backcountry skiing, minus the skinning. Its dozen or so named territories—mostly sprawling glade districts—each have distinct temperaments.

“It can take two or three visits before guests get a feel for the mountain,” claims Vern Barber, Bohemia’s general manager.

I spend one morning adrift in one of the territories, Extreme Backcountry, a half-mile-wide expanse of Bohemia’s toughest terrain. Its high-angle tree runs, cliff drops, and narrow chutes kept funneling me onto unexpected lines. Supposedly, somewhere out there is a frozen waterfall drop I never managed to find. I wasn’t going to hit it. I just wanted to look.

Now I’m farther out in Middle Earth, another territory, surfing Boho’s longest runs through twisting hardwoods. Less steep, but somehow more exhausting. This is where skiers come to explore, hunting for pockets of untouched powder.

It has been revealed that I stop at a trail marked “Helm’s Deep.” It took several attempts to find this place. Even then, it felt like an accident. The entrance is just a gap interrupting the tangle of trees—my only way down. Two clicks of my poles, and I drop in.

Dry powder explodes on my first turn. Branches rake both sleeves as I weave between trunks. Each bank hides what lies ahead. I barrel over a blind rise straight toward a stand of maples. I slash hard right and spray snow against the bark. Off balance, I slip through a drift and down a steep-sided gully.

Industry observers note that “You’re rowdy,” I grunt as the trees finally open. With room to breathe, I find my rhythm. Ahead lie 30 yards of untracked pillows. I point my tips and charge.

By the time I pop out at the bottom, a throng of skiers is already waiting. Not for a chairlift, but for a bus. Bohemia’s farthest backcountry runs spill onto Lac La Belle Road, where a fleet of buses collects those who make it out of the woods. Over four days, I’ve shuffled through far more bus lines than lift lines. With luck, the next shuttle will be the elusive ABBA bus, plastered with Swedish memorabilia and bumping “Dancing Queen.” Today, I’m not so lucky. I climb into a regular bus for the day’s last ride, legs shot.

As we pull into base, the parking lot is just getting started. Around a fire barrel, a haggard congregation passes bottles and joints. Skiers still in bibs boil noodles on camp stoves between RVs and Sprinter vans. This crowd feels familiar—as if every little ski hill I grew up on in Michigan sent its most adventurous regulars.

The village itself is a jumble of yurts, stitched together by gangways. It houses bars, a hostel, and a surprisingly elaborate Nordic spa. Its 30-person hot tub was dubbed “dude stew.” But Vern claims they don’t call it that anymore.

Industry observers note that for a place that wears you out by noon, Boho has a strange amount of energy after dark. Inside the North Pole Bar, skiers running on beer and pasties belt out “Country Roads” with the band. The party stumbles outside to packed pools and saunas. Much later, some hooligans will hike halfway up the frontside and sled down on stolen cafeteria trays. I am one of them.

According to recent reports, on my last morning at Mount Bohemia, a particularly nasty blizzard has blown in off Lake Superior. Word is spreading through the yurts: high winds and whiteout have shut down the lifts. The buses aren’t running.

It has been revealed that skiers gather at the back of the village, their helmets and jackets already covered in powder. Out of the blowing snow, a single snowcat materializes. Vern himself is behind the wheel. The wind forces him to park at an angle to wrestle the door open. Skiers cram aboard, a handful at a time, bound for the summit.

It has been revealed that I join the others in line. We laugh and curse as the snowcat is swallowed again by the whiteout. Powder is piling up around our shins. Above us, the glades are already buried. I can’t feel my toes. It’s a perfect day.

Not a bad place for a pilgrimage.

#79189. The Pentagon Wants Public Lands ‘Offered Up’ for a New Army Base. Wyoming Is Interested

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (606 w)

The Pentagon Wants Public Lands ‘Offered Up’ for a New Army Base. Wyoming Is Interested

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (606 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a latest military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.
  • Sources indicate that the base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest.
  • Hegseth noted the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth wants to build a latest military base, and some public land states like Wyoming say they have just the spots.

Sources indicate that the base would house between 15,000 and 25,000 active-duty service members, according to a red, white and blue competition flier for what Hegseth is calling the Next Great American Base contest. And ideally it would include 100,000 to 250,000 contiguous acres.

Hegseth noted the base should be a “dynamic, self-sustaining power projection platform” with its own power generation, modern air defenses, and advanced technology, reported Newsweek in early October, when the call for pitches first arrived. He went on to say the best proposals would cut through “the red tape, offering up the land and rolling out the red carpet for our military families.”.

But much of the “red tape” associated with building a base on hundreds of thousands of acres of unoccupied land is likely federal government red tape. And no clear path at the moment exists for how to requisition and build a fresh military installation on federal public land, noted Mark Squillace, a natural resources law professor at the University of Colorado Law School.

In a recent development, the Department of Defense would need to work around current Bureau of Land Management or U.S. Forest Service management plans that include stipulations for wildlife like migration corridors and winter range closures.

It’s also unclear if the base needs to support the U.S. Navy, which would limit public-land options since the bulk of the country’s public lands are in the Interior West like Nevada, Idaho and Utah, though the fact sheet states all locations, even those without water access, are on the table.

The DOD already administers 8.4 million acres in the U.S., but is looking to acquire lands managed by other agencies.

Sources indicate that wyoming, for its part, is eyeing both state and federal land for the base. The state’s adjutant general, Maj. Gen. Greg Porter, told a legislative committee in early November that Wyoming has identified at least four “chunks” of state and federal land, as reported by the Cowboy State Daily last week. Which chunks have not yet been disclosed.

Squillace lined out how building a military base on public land could — or could not — become a reality.

It has been revealed that the DOD would first likely need to discuss any public land acquisition with the BLM or Forest Service. If the land use agency agrees that a military base would fit the current land management plan, it would need to prepare a draft Environmental Impact Statement that brings up potential complications and confirms compliance with laws like the Endangered Species Act or National Historic Preservation Act.

Industry observers note that “A positive review would likely lead to temporary withdrawal of the land from the operation of certain public land laws (like mining and leasing) that could interfere with the operation of the base,” Squillace indicates, while also noting that existing rights would be protected. Any particularly valuable mining claims would have to be bought out in what he describes as a “time consuming and expensive” process.

Read Next: Senate Poised to Vote on Affordability Package that Hunters, Anglers Worry Is a Trojan Horse for Public-Land Rollbacks.

Ultimately, however, Squillace indicates any large-scale, long-term use of land would likely need to be approved by Congress, “since such transfers of public land are not authorized under law.”  Whether or not the dramatically different Congress to be sworn in next year would green light a public-land transfer requested by Hegseth also remains uncertain.

#79188. ‘Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (831 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outdoorlife ↗ Open Full Page

‘Complete Shock.’ Long-Haul Trucker Hunter Tags 227-Inch Nontypical During State Park Hunt

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (831 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure.
  • It has been revealed that “I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life.
  • Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indiana’s state park system offers a limited draw hunt that allows residents to target the abundant whitetails on park land that doesn’t get much hunting pressure. There are about 25 parks in the popular program, with two firearms hunts allowed on most of them. Each hunt runs just two days.

It has been revealed that “I put in for the early two-day hunt on November 16 and 17 at a Northeast Indiana state park and got drawn for it,” Mike Miltroka tells Outdoor Life. “Trail cameras are not allowed on park [land]. But you can scout before hunt days. I scouted the park on Sunday, the day before the first day of hunting on November 16.”.

Miltroka found a likely spot and, well before daybreak on Monday, he was in a tree saddle with his Ruger American Generation II chambered in 7mm PRC.

“It was cool and a little windy, but I was seeing deer soon after daybreak,” indicates Miltroka, a 38-year-old long-haul truck driver from Farmland. “I spotted a good buck far out, but the cover was too thick to shoot.”.

Recent findings suggest that as the morning wore on, Miltroka got a chance to take two does, and he dropped them both with his Ruger. He toted both does to his truck using a deer cart, since motorized vehicles are not allowed off-road.

The spot was already paying off, and Miltroka had a friend — who had seen a giant deer using the area before the hunt — to thank for tipping him off about it.

“I’d never seen the deer previously, but a buddy highlighted me a video [he’d taken] of the buck a month earlier while visiting the park … It was a place no one else was hunting, and I checked to make sure it was okay to hunt there – and it was.”.

On the second day of the hunt, Miltroka chose a different tree. He climbed into a substantial walnut closer to the cover where he’d seen the buck on Monday. But unlike the day before, Miltroka didn’t see much except a coyote. Then, around 8:30, things changed.

“I heard something raking trees behind me, and I didn’t know what it was. I kept trying to see what was making all that racket, then I saw him out about 70 yards,” he notes. “I knew it was a good shooter buck, and when I got him in my scope I squeezed the trigger, fired, and the deer took off running.”.

Miltroka jacked another round into the chamber, but as soon as he picked up the running buck in his scope again, the deer went down.

It wasn’t until Miltroka studied the dead buck through his scope that he realized how immense the deer was.

Sources indicate that “I started shaking, and yelling,” he indicates. “I got buck fever after it was over … I called a friend of mine and was so excited he asked if I was tied tight to my tree, and I said yes. I was shaking so much I might have fallen out of it.”.

Once he was steady enough, Miltroka climbed down and walked up on the deer.

Recent findings suggest that “I was in complete shock,” he notes. “I’ve only taken about six bucks, and none even have the size of this one. I was screaming with joy.”.

In a recent development, he filled out a transport tag for his buck, which filled his limit of three deer for the park hunt – only one of which can be a buck. Then he wheeled the buck to his vehicle, loaded it, and drove to park headquarters to check it in.

Recent findings suggest that the buck’s field dressed weight was 181 pounds. The 22-point nontypical was green scored by an official Boone & Crockett measurer the day after Miltroka shot it. It gross scored 227 inches, with a net score of 197 6/8s inches. It has an outside antler spread of nearly 25 inches, and one main beam of the rack measures over 27 inches.

He will have the buck scored again after the required 60-day drying period for B&C and will enter the buck into B&C’s nontypical record category. He’ll also submit his buck to the Hoosier Record Buck Program.

“The park hunts are well run and there are plenty of deer,” says Miltroka. “I saw lots of deer being checked in during the hunts and some nice bucks.

#79187. The Best Cellular Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

The Best Cellular Trail Cameras of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 22 min read (4303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fieldandstream

⏱️ ~22 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that for the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot.
  • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
  • Recent findings suggest that I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that for the best overall performance, the Moultrie Edge 4 Solar and Browning Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV share the top spot. For hunters on a budget, the SpyPoint Flex-M2 is the pick. Need maximum detection range, choose the Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0. For the sharpest images, the Stealth Cam Deceptor Max 3.0 leads the field.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve been running trail cameras since film-based models were all the rage in the early 1990s. I remember walking laps around the local Walmart, waiting for the one-hour photo lab to process my prints. Most of the time, it was 24 images of a branch that the wind blew back and forth. Occasionally, I’d get a deer—sometimes even a good buck.

In a recent development, trail cams have come a long way since, and, of course, cellular trail cameras dominate the scene today. If you want to learn all you can about the critters you hunt without setting foot in the woods other than to change batteries or move a camera or two, cellular trail cameras are the way to go. But which cell cams?

To help you figure out which models are right for you, I spent two months running and testing the latest newly introduced-for-2026 cell cams in my backyard and on a nearby 700-acre whitetail property in Colorado. Testing conditions were difficult. Every camera was exposed to heavy wind, a 60-day average high temperature of 95.7 degrees, rain, and hail that damaged roofs. The good news: There were no flops. I would have no reservations running any of the new cellular cams below anywhere in the country. That noted, some proved better than others depending on what your value most. So, let’s dive in. Here are the best cellular trail cameras of 2026.

Sources indicate that one complaint I’ve always had about cellular trail cameras is the antennas, as they are always breaking off in backpacks or the back seat of my truck. Mother Nature has her way with them, dropping dead branches and crushing skinny, side-mounted antennas. I’ve even broken a couple by catching the antenna in my pant leg while walking to a stand in the dark.

Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV features an innovative, wide, blade-style antenna located in the center of the trail camera. It’s extra-sturdy and folds back and locks into the back of the main camera housing for easy, secure transport. The high-gain antenna also grabbed the most available network more swiftly than any other camera in this year’s test.

The MAX HD DV uses the same straightforward interface on the camera’s lower housing behind the lock-and-latch door that Browning people are used to and appreciate. The 1.5-inch LED screen is bright, and the soft-push buttons don’t stick. When you turn the camera on, the LED screen displays a 10-second countdown before you close the door.

Recent findings suggest that you have plenty of options when setting up the camera via the Strike Fore Wireless app. I recommend running the camera on Medium photo quality with High video. Avoid the Ultra-quality setting for both photo and video to save battery life, as the quality is plenty good without it. All images are delivered in HD, so there are no grainy thumbnails or waiting for the camera to trigger again to view a high-resolution photo. Videos with audio are ultra-clean. The camera took very few false triggers, and I love the user-adjustable flash.

Sources indicate that over 60 days in the field, Browning’s Defender Pro Scout MAX HD DV captured deer, day and night, in the center of the frame from 10 feet to 120 feet. Browning lists a detection range of 100 feet, but this camera exceeds that distance.

In a recent development, using just 8 standard alkaline batteries, camera life was excellent, holding at around 90 percent after 60 days afield. At night, the MAX HD DV uses Illuma-Smart technology to adjust the flash for crisp, clear nighttime images, and its detection range remains over 100 feet after dark. This trail camera was built to handle extreme weather and keep delivering images.

The only area Browning Trail Cameras needs to improve upon is its Strike Force Wireless app. The app functions well but struggles to categorize photos in the main image Library when you’re running more than one camera.

It has been revealed that other than that, Browning’s upcoming MAX HD DV is everything I want in a cellular trail camera. It captures HD photos and 1080p video with audio, doesn’t spook deer, and has given me zero hassles after 60 days afield. It’s a tad pricey, but you’ll more than make up for it in batteries.

Moultrie’s Edge 4 Solar is the best solar-powered cellular trail camera I’ve ever used, and, at $169.99—including the solar panel—it is priced right. The panel itself is simple and effective; it slides and locks into the top of the camera, and you can angle the it to ensure it gathers as much sunlight as possible throughout the day.

Recent findings suggest that I’ve had two Edge 4 Solar cameras in the field longer than any other cellular trail camera in this year’s test. They were the first cameras delivered to my doorstep, and when I get a new product, I like to start using it right away. Using Moultrie’s $50 (aftermarket) Power Mag II battery pack in tandem with the solar panel, my battery life has never dipped below 80 percent. This means you can stay out of the woods and reduce your human footprint, which is the main goal of cellular trail cameras.

Sources indicate that setup is super easy. Like all the trail cameras in this year’s test, the Edge 4 Solar connects to the strongest available cellular network. I like the latest internal interface. The white push up/down, on/off button is gone. Moultrie added a twist-and-turn dial that doesn’t stick. The battery life indicator is back, and once powered on, all three lights (Not Connected-red, Connecting-yellow, Connected-green) turn solid. Then, the Connecting light flashes slowly, and after about one minute, the green Connected light turns solid green. At this point, the camera is fully operational. It pairs seamlessly with Moultrie’s app and is one of the most user-friendly cellular trail cameras in this year’s test.

Aside from the latest interface, Moultrie made other changes that earned the new Edge 4 Solar our top honor. The most notable is better nighttime image quality and a reduction in false triggers. Moultrie’s new Night Clarity feature uses enhanced low-glow IR LEDs to help illuminate the backdrop and boost edge-to-edge sharpness. Nighttime images are excellent, and every image, day or night, is delivered in HD.

It has been revealed that last year, especially toward the end of my 60-day testing period, my Edge 3 started triggering when nothing was there. The Edge 4 Pro Solar has not followed suit.

Sources indicate that another new and purposeful feature is Buck Shot. Moultrie AI technology detects mature bucks and sends a zoomed-in, max-resolution image. I really enjoyed this feature. Typically, action on my lease doesn’t heat up until mid-October, as few bucks summer on the property. However, this year has been different. A pair of shooter bucks—bucks I passed last fall—are semi-regular on an oat field. The Edge 4 Solar sends me a zoomed-in picture every single time either buck trips the camera.

Recent findings suggest that in a partnership with onX, Edge 4 cameras are instantly pinned the second they are placed. By the end of September, I will have multiple trail cameras—cellular and conventional—spread across the West and Midwest. Too often, I get in a hurry and forget to drop a camera pin when I’m using trail cameras. However, if I’m using Moultrie, I can forget, and the map-pinning technology saves me.

Other standout features of the Edge 4 Solar include a tough-as-nails housing with an IP67 waterproof rating. Both of my Edge 4 Solar cameras have been exposed to torrential downpours and hail. Not a drop of moisture has gotten inside, and after months in the field, the cameras and the panels look like they just came out of the box.

Sources indicate that at under $80, SpyPoint’s Flex-M2 is a solid cellular trail camera. It comes with a two-year warranty, and SpyPoint offers a pair of M2s for just $129.99, which is an excellent deal.

My first experience with the Flex-M2 was in Montana while helping a buddy set up his whitetail property. The Flex-M2 is compact, lightweight, easy to set up, and connects to the strongest cellular network in the area. Its .4-second advertised trigger speed proved accurate and reliable in my testing, and the camera captured deer at distances beyond 90 feet.

Sources indicate that when I returned from Montana, I added a pair of Flex-M2 cameras to my Colorado property. Both have been on the property for 60 days and send crisp images and 1080p video with solid audio to my phone daily. They have withstood torrid summer heat, rain and hail, and continue to impress me.

One problem I’ve had with both cameras is battery life. Using standard AA alkaline batteries, both Flex-M2 models drained relatively swiftly. That said, when I swapped the battery trays for SpyPoint’s LIT-22 rechargeable power packs, battery life improved significantly. Set to Photo-only mode with medium photo resolution and a multi-shot setting of two images per trigger, my battery life has been holding steady above 80 percent.

It has been revealed that setup and connection time was straightforward and quick. I like the positive bottom latch lock, and the raised, gridded on/off switch is easy to operate. Once clicked on, the cellular lights blink until the camera receives a signal. Next, the status light turns blue. Once connected, the blue LED extinguishes, and the green LED on the outside of the camera blinks for 10 seconds. Once the green light stops flashing, the camera is in transmission mode.

The Flex-M2 was the smallest cellular trail cam in this year’s test, and the long antenna is detachable for easy transport. Once you place your M2 in the field, it immediately reveals up on the SpyPoint app map feature.

Industry observers note that the camera occasionally produces false triggers, but I was able to reduce this by setting the sensitivity to Medium, and the camera still picks up deer-sized game beyond 90 feet. The BuckTracker feature has done its job. Buck pics are slugged correctly, and I’ve yet to have the technology slug a doe as a buck. BuckTracker even correctly identified and a 3-inch spick at 64 feet.

In the end, Spypoint’s Flex-M2 gets our 2026 Best Value award because while it might not have all the bells and whistles of other cell scouters, it does the job—and does it for about half the price of several others.

Last year, Tactacam’s Reveal Ultra took home top honors in our cellular trail camera test. Its predecessor, the Reveal Pro 4.0, nearly earned the cell-cam maker a repeat performance, but fell just a tad short. It is, however, a cell scouter that every hunter should take a close look at.

Industry observers note that like the Ultra, the Pro 4.0 features Low-Glow and No-Glow flash settings. I love this option. Low-Glow works great for fields, logging roads, or any camera location where detection range needs a bump. No-Glow is ideal for tight timber trail crossings, river crossings, scrapes, or any area where detection range matters less and stealth matters more. The Reveal Pro 4.0 doesn’t spook deer. When set in No-Glow, deer don’t even glance at the camera, and new Dual Image Sensors improve day and nighttime photos.

Another stealth boost is that the slight click that previous Reveal models produced when capturing a nighttime image is gone. According to Reveal, the Dual Sensors—one stacked on top of the other—produce cleaner nighttime images without the audible click associated with a low-light filter. Once you set the Reveal Pro 4.0 in the woods, it’s a ghost, which is just what you want.

In a recent development, battery life on last year’s Ultra model was solid and given that the Reveal app lets users select camera sensitivity levels between 0 and 9, false triggers have always been few and far between. However, Reveal wanted the Pro 4.0 to have a longer run time, especially when battery-draining features such as larger image sizes, longer video durations, and Live View Mode are used.

The battery-life boosting answer is Reveal’s FlexPack R5 and R10 Power Systems. The latest interface location on the camera’s right side, in the upper-right corner, lets the bottom of the camera (the battery box) pull away. The design was well thought out and is an overlooked feature of the new Pro 4.0. With the battery box removed, aftermarket R5 (5,000 mAh) and R10 (10,000 mAh) Power Systems plug in much like rechargeable batteries found on power tools.

Sources indicate that I ran the camera for 15 days using standard Alkaline AA batteries and for 15 days using the FlexPack R5. There is no question the Power Systems increase battery life and are worth the money. During its 15-day run time, the 4.0 with R5 triggered 332 times. I requested 28 videos and purposely activated Live View 10 times to further test battery life. At the end of the test, the camera still had 95 percent battery life remaining.

One small blip with this camera is that of all the cellular models I tested, the Pro 4.0 had the slowest connection time. I ran a pair of Pro 4.0s, and the average time from powering on the cameras to receiving my first test photo in an area with 4 bars of AT&T 5G LTE service was 12 minutes. I’m not sure what that was about, but both cameras struggled to get a signal and start transmitting images. Once the camera were fully connected, though, trigger speed was excellent, detection range was spot-on, and images and videos were clear and colorful.

If it weren’t for the SpyPoint’s crazy-low price, Stealth Cam’s Deceptor Max 3.0 would have won our Best Photo Quality and Best Value awards. At just under $120, this cellular trail camera should be on every hunter’s radar. Past Stealth Cam cellular models I’ve test produced too many false triggers and had relatively poor battery life. Not so with this one. After 60 days in the field, the Deceptor Max 3.0 has sent only three images to my phone that didn’t show a deer, thanks to the camera’s latest False Trigger Filter feature, and after 723 photos and 23 20-second videos, the battery is at 90 percent.

With its No Glow flash, the Max 3.0 has not spooked deer, near or far. Trigger speed is excellent, and with the Command app and the camera set to Standard blur reduction, images have been crisp and clean. The camera captured a doe blazing past at 1:30 a.m. in the center of the frame. The doe was in focus, and 15 seconds later, so were a pair of coyotes hot on her trail.

The Deceptor Max 3.0 lets users set photo quality to 50MP. That makes for really good pics, but it’s more than most folks need and eats up battery life. I tested the camera at 4MP and 8MP, and the Max 3.0 produced the clearest, brightest, and most colorful images in this year’s test.

Industry observers note that A cool feature that Stealth Cam added is Rack Alert, which sends a message to your smartphone letting you know the exact moment a racked deer steps in front of your Max 3.0. This feature worked great on my Colorado lease, and my Oklahoma buddy purchased three Max 3.0 cameras and set them over feeders. He told me he never looks at his image library until Rack Alert informs him. He trusts the technology, and so do I.

Upgraded antenna pulls poor cell service.

The solar cord is big, long, and clunky.

The Interceptor is not newly introduced for this year, but it one of our favorites from last year’s test, winning our Best Trigger Speed award. Covert upped its game 2025, producing a new solar cell cam scouter that’s lightning fast and offers tons of great features. The Interceptor Solar was easy to set up. Downloading the Covert app, building an account, and getting the cam operational took less than five minutes.

Sources indicate that the camera’s paddle-style antenna proved rigid and robust, even in heavy winds. Covert lists the trigger speed at .4 seconds, but my testing revealed an average of .24 seconds. That data was obtained using two different stopwatches, as well as a chip time card that runners use.

It has been revealed that when charged to full, the camera’s on-board solar keeps the unit running, even in dense timber. Several times, the Interceptor got down to less than 30 percent battery life at night, but it would still center images in the frame, and deliver good-qualiy photos and real-time 2K video. During the day, even without direct sun exposure, battery life would rise to 80 percent. When set on a pond and alfalfa plot, the battery never dipped below 60 percent and would achieve a full charge during the day.

Covert lists the effective flash range at 90 feet, and my testing confirmed this. I appreciate the 2-inch screen, though very little of the actual setup work is accomplished using the camera. Everything is done in the Covert app. The Covert Interceptor Solar features on-board GPS, so you can’t lose your camera, uses 8 AA batteries as backup, and comes with a 2-year warranty.

My only complaint on this otherwise excellent camera is the long and bulky cord that connects the on-board solar unit to the camera. Be sure to take some Gorilla tape or some zip-ties to roll the cord up and tuck it out of the way. But that’s the end of my quibbling. The camera took only 11 false images during its 20-day testing period and captured a full-sprint coyote in the center of the frame, with no blur. The camera does have species recognition, which works well, but it is a service that costs extra, and I would deactivate it. Like most hunters, I know what a doe and buck deer look like.

Requires a minimum of two cameras.

Longer setup and deployment time.

Cuddeback continues to offer it’s CuddeLink system. The nice thing about Cuddelink is that once you have the Home camera and a cellular strategy, you can run as many as 24 cameras on that same plan, which sarts as low as $10 per month. I opted for the $40 plan to receive unlimited photos. I tested the CuddeLink L-Series Cell Home unit ($130) and CuddeLink L-Seires cell cam ($150), so my initial investment was more. Still, I could add additional CuddeLink-compatible cell cameras (up to 24) to my $40 per month plan.

Industry observers note that operationally, the Home (CuddeLink) and Remote (L-Series) systems are sound. However, you’ll need to read heavy instruction manuals to get them linked to the same chain and go through the settings. It’s not a problem, and it’s not difficult. However, it will take you some time to learn the ins and outs of the system. This duo took much longer to learn about and get in the field than other cameras. That stated, one the initial system is setup, it’s easy to add more cams and daisy chain them into the system.

The CuddeLink L-Series comes in multiple models. I tested the Zoom IR. The photo quality is only decent, but what I do like about the camera is that it uses a center-angle Fresnel lens that increases detection range and zooms the photo in. I’m not in love with having the Home camera and then linking cameras to it, especially cellular, but the system does work and does have the potential to save you money.

Internal screen viewer to aid setup.

Among the most simple setups in the test.

Night pics suffer a bit at longer ranges.

This camera is not new by any means, but don’t let that stop you. High-quality photos, a lightning-fast trigger, and easy setup are a massive pluses with the CelluCore Live. The impressive 0.2-second trigger speed helps capture sharp images and can keep up with fast-moving deer. Plus, the fast image recovery time and subtle infrared flash elevate this cam to the next level. The only thing keeping this camera from the top models is a moderate detection range, and the data plans are, well, not much. It’s not cheap either, though you may be able to find deals.

Thanks to some fantastic friends, I have access to over 700 acres of prime Colorado whitetail dirt, which has proven to be the perfect testing ground for our annual cellular trail camera test. There are plenty of deer to get pictures of and a combination of summer heat, thunderstorms, wind, and extreme temperature fluctuations tests the cameras’ durability.

Since I conducted last year’s cellular trail camera test, I had all the apps on my smartphone. All I did was add cameras, adjust sensitivity levels, check connectivity, and dial in the settings. For testing, I set all cameras to photo resolutions between 4 and 8MP, 1080p video, and two images per trigger.

Recent findings suggest that before field deployment, I tested all the cams in my backyard. I wanted to make sure they paired with their corresponding app and that photos were transmitting. I set cones at measured distances and walked, jogged, and sprinted past each camera at 10-foot intervals, from 20 to 120 feet. I repeated this process in the field as well. I tested trigger speed and detection zines during daylight and nighttime hours.

In the field, I rotated all the cameras between four areas: a three-way trail intersection, the lower end of an alfalfa plot, a pond, and a community scrape deer use year-round. Throughout the test—over the course of 60 days—I evaluated each camera’s durability, ease of setup, price, battery life, image and video quality, detection range, and trigger speed. Finally, when all the testing and evaluating is done, I picked our winners.

Sources indicate that ease of setup and quick connection to the camera’s corresponding app save time and frustration. Not every hunter is a tech wizard, and thanks to the simplicity of this year’s camera crop, you don’t have to be. The only camera I had to fight with in terms of connectivity and transmission was the Reveal Pro 4.0. However, that fight was minor.

Many cell-cam makers are skipping grainy thumbnails and going straight to all-HD all the time. I like this. Cell cams have made me very impatient. When I get a picture of a buck, I don’t want to download a grainy image to my computer and then study it for hours trying to determine whether the buck is a shooter while I wait for a high-resolution image to come through. Cams that automatically send hi-res pics get bonus points in my book. Choose a cellular trail camera that lets you adjust image and video quality and set both high enough to avoid compromising image quality but not so high that battery life suffers.

Trigger speed matters, especially during the rut. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have rapid trigger speed, quicker recovery times, and some type of anti-blur technology. Summertime deer don’t often test a camera’s trigger speed, but during the rut, when a doe comes running past, you want that doe centered in the frame, and the camera needs to recover fast enough that the big buck hot on her heels gets his picture taken too. The cellular trail cameras I tested this year have fast triggers and quick recovery times.

I prefer cellular trail cameras with an adjustable flash. Some come with adjustable flash settings, while others adjust the flash setting automatically based on the time of day. Stay away from high-glow LEDs and any cell camera that produces a flash that spooks deer. All the cameras I tested this year didn’t bother deer a bit.

Recent findings suggest that cellular trail-cam manufacturers embellish a lot of things. One thing they don’t embellish—or at least didn’t embellish this year, is detection range. If anything, they underplayed it. Detection range is the maximum distance at which a camera will detect an object. Typically, the farther an object is from the camera, the larger it needs to be to be detected by the camera. Anything at over 100 feet is impressive.

I like a very basic and straightforward app that allows me immediate access to the camera’s settings. I like to try all the technologies and features of every cell camera I test. The better the app, the easier it is to swap between settings, organize photos, etc. Many of today’s cellular trail cameras have fancy features. Take advantage of them and see if you find them beneficial. Some of them drain battery life; others don’t. Find out what works best for you and the area you hunt.

I Went Duck Hunting During the Infamous Armistice Day Storm, and Lived to Tell About It

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3071 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 problem of Outdoor Life.
  • There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.
  • It started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This story, “Cold as Death,” appeared in the October 1955 problem of Outdoor Life.

There has never been anything along the upper Mississippi, before or since, like the Armistice Day storm of 1940.

It started out as a mild, cloudy morning with the temperature between 50 and 60. Fellows went duck hunting in shirt sleeves. The wind picked up velocity as the day went along, but not enough to get excited about — not until late afternoon. Then, with little warning, a full-scale prairie blizzard screamed in out of the northwest.

By dark the air was smoking with gale-driven snow, and the thermometer plunged near zero. Bitter winds blew all night. The weather experts remarked afterward that gusts hit 80 miles an hour. The storm laid a track of death and destruction across six states; it pounded ships to pieces on the Great Lakes, blocked roads, isolated towns, paralyzed cities, and buried cars. Hundreds were marooned on highways. A crack streamliner was 27 hours late into Minneapolis. And when the morning of November 12 broke, 20 duck hunters lay dead, frozen in stiff, grotesque poses — scattered on mud bars, sand spits, and willow-grown islands of the Mississippi bottoms between Red Wing, Minnesota, and La Crosse, Wisconsin.

I was among the luckier ones. I spent that terrible night with two companions under an overturned skiff on a mud bar — wet from head to foot, without fire or heavy clothing, pants frozen to my legs, and kept alive only by the body warmth of the men who lay huddled on both sides of me. The storm cost me six weeks of agony in a hospital and half of my left foot. But at least I survived.

I was 14 at the time, attending high school in my home town of Winona, Minnesota. We got out of classes at 11 o’clock because it was Armistice Day. I scurried for home, planning an afternoon of duck hunting.

The wind was already fairly fresh and mother was uneasy. “The storm warnings are up,” she told me while getting my lunch. But I grew up in Winona and knew the river, and at that age, bad weather didn’t worry me. The only thing it meant to me was good shooting. Ducks had been scarce all fall and maybe a blow would bring ’em down. So I hurried through lunch, impatient to get in a blind.

It has been revealed that while I was loading my gear in the car, my cousin, Bob Stephens, highlighted up with a partner, Cal Wieczorek, and they decided to join me. Bob was 20, Cal about 19.

We drove to the Prairie Island spillway at the lower end of the Winona pool, where Dad kept his boat. It was a 16-footer, pointed at both ends, with a homemade bracket for an outboard. We decided to hunt a place known as the Firing Line, along the border of the Upper Mississippi Wildlife Refuge, three or four miles upstream. Hunters lined up there to intercept ducks flying in and out of the refuge. In stormy weather the pass-shooting was exceptionally good, and this looked like that kind of day.

The wind was blowing half a gale now and was beginning to bite. Ominous dark clouds raced overhead, and scuds of cold rain pelted down as we clamped our old three-horse outboard on the boat, cranked it up, and headed out into the choppy pool. The three of us were a heavy load, and the skiff made slow headway against the wind.

We didn’t give it a thought then, but we couldn’t have been more poorly prepared. I was wearing cotton clothes — pants, shirt, socks, and a jacket lighter than a hunting coat. I had overshoes over my leather shoes. Bob and Cal were dressed similarly, except for hip boots. Cal and I had gloves. Bob had a heavy raincoat, and I still believe that made the difference between living and dying for me.

We had one book of matches and no pocketknife. I was carrying a 16 gauge single-barrel Winchester; the other two had pumps. Because we intended to pass-shoot, we took no decoys.

According to recent reports, backed up by a series of low dams, the Mississippi is two to three miles wide in that section, flooding its bottoms and forming open lakes, meandering channels, small islands, bars, and rush beds. We threaded our way through this maze, wallowing in the heavy seas. It took us 1½ hours to cover the distance to the Firing Line.

It has been revealed that the sky was full of ducks; they were barreling across the bottoms in crazy skeins, riding the wind, and turning and twisting below treetop height. It was plain they didn’t like the weather. Before the afternoon was over I actually swung at a greenhead with my gun as he hovered above my head, almost stationary, while bucking the gale.

In a recent development, when we finally got to the Firing Line it was too crowded. The blinds were only about 25 yards apart and all occupied. Ducks were rocketing back and forth over the marsh and there was a steady barrage of shooting. We decided to find another spot.

Recent findings suggest that by the time we found it — on a willow-covered island with many rushes in front — we were beginning to lose interest. The wind was howling like a banshee, down off the high bluffs to the west, with sleet and fine snow in its teeth. We hunkered in the willows for almost an hour, killed four ducks, and decided we’d had enough. The cold was already bone-chilling, our hands were so stiff we could hardly handle our guns, and we were starting to worry about getting back to the landing.

Recent findings suggest that two strangers came by in a little duck boat; they told us they were scared. That settled it for us, but going home was easier said than done. None of us knew exactly where we were, and when we tried to shove away from shore, the seas threatened to swamp us. We finally dragged the skiff to the lee side and managed to get it afloat and start the motor. But before going 200 yards we ran aground on a mud bar, which we couldn’t skirt because of the wind and seas. We dragged the boat across the bar and started on again.

Recent findings suggest that we did that about four times before finding ourselves by a big open slough and admitting we were lost. It was almost dark now and snowing so hard we couldn’t see 100 feet. We couldn’t even look into the wind — the storm cut our eyeballs like a sandblast. And the slough was a welter of dirty foaming water in which our skiff probably wouldn’t last more than a minute.

While we debated what to do, another boat loomed out of the stormy dusk, riding low with four hunters. Two of them were only a little older than I — one from my home room at school. The others were men who had hunted the river bottoms all their lives. When they stated they knew the way to Prairie Island and could make it without swamping, we decided to follow.

In a recent development, but I couldn’t get the outboard started. Bob and Cal rowed, handicapped by cold-numbed hands, while I tinkered with it. We managed to keep the other boat in sight for a few minutes. Then, pitching and rolling, it disappeared and we didn’t see it again. When our frantic yells brought no answer we realized we were again on our own. It was days before we learned what happened to the other party. Their skiff had capsized when we lost sight of it. Three of the hunters died there, standing in the icy water, not knowing which way to go to dry land. By some miracle one of the boys survived the night and rescue parties found him on a near-by island at daybreak.

In a recent development, only a few minutes after we lost that boat we were washed ashore on a sand spit. Bob and Cal leaped clear as we grounded and escaped a wetting. I was in the stern of the skiff, working on the outboard — right in the path of a wicked sea that smashed over us the instant we touched bottom.

It has been revealed that I can’t describe the shock that icy dunking gave me. I clawed my way out of the swamped boat, and the wind cut like a braided whip. My legs wouldn’t hold me up, so I crawled across the mud until I was beyond reach of the waves and lay there, cold and weak.

Cal and Bob dragged the boat up on dry land, turned it over, and propped one side up to make a shelter. When they finished I crawled under it. My pants and jacket crackled as I moved. They had frozen stiff in the few minutes I lay exposed to the wind.

We still had only a vague idea of our location, but we knew that large open lake, which we couldn’t cross in our puny skiff, lay between us and any landing. We didn’t talk much about it; we didn’t need to. Live or die, we’d have to spend the night where we were.

It has been revealed that bob and Cal did everything possible. They gathered rushes and put them under the boat to keep me off the wet mud. Then they searched desperately for firewood, but there wasn’t so much as a scrub willow. They finally found a few pieces of water-logged driftwood, heaped them in a pyramid, and turned the outboard motor up to drain gas on it — a risky thing to do, except in a desperate emergency like ours. But the screaming wind whipped the gas into nowhere as fast as it ran out of the tank. They struck one match after another without getting a spark of fire.

The last match flared and died in the darkness, and they crawled under the boat and lay down on the wet rushes, one on each side of me. They spread their hunting coats over us and laid Bob’s raincoat on top. The raincoat kept the worst of the wind out and probably saved me from freezing.

Industry observers note that we had little sense of time and hardly talked. Bob told me afterward that I spoke only two or three times during the night, and then I worried about the anxiety my parents must be feeling.

Recent findings suggest that I shivered for what seemed like hours, with my hands wedged between my thighs, since that seemed to be the warmest place on my body. I prayed silently. I didn’t think much about dying. I believed we’d get through the night somehow and in the morning find our way home. I realized finally that all feeling was gone in my feet; they were wooden stumps, no longer a part of me. I must have dozed, for I recall waking up and feeling warm, but that lasted only a minute or two and then I was shivering again.

The thing I remember best was the unending scream of the wind. It never stopped raging — searching under the overturned boat, wailing, screeching, terribly alive, terribly cold.

In a recent development, sometime in the night Bob remembered that he had two apples and two sandwiches in his hunting coat. They were frozen hard, but we gnawed at them and they seemed to help.

The sound of distant gunshots reached us several times, and once we thought we heard faint, far-off yells for help. But our own guns were so crusted with ice that we couldn’t fire them, and it was useless to shout.

Industry observers note that we knew we weren’t the only hunters lost on the river bottom. Others were enduring the same torture. And we felt sure there must be rescue parties trying to find us, but we didn’t think we could count on them while the storm continued.

It was days before we learned all that happened that hard night. Rescue efforts began at dark, and men fought the storm and seas all night in skiffs and powerboats. Some even waded the sloughs to bring lost men to shore. It wasn’t a night for small craft, and no one will ever know how many boats were overturned, swamped, and driven back. But the search went on, hour after hour, heedless of the wind, cold, and snow.

Industry observers note that the night was an awful ordeal for the hunters. One party huddled on a marshy island beside a fire started with dead grass and fed with more than 40 cedar decoys. Gas from an outboard was used to rekindle the blaze each time it died down. Another group marched, jumped, and sparred around a fire built from their boats. Still another found a patch of timber, got a fire going, and then shot dead branches off trees for fuel.

It has been revealed that they were the lucky ones; others didn’t fare so well. Two died under an overturned boat, unable to see a bonfire 400 yards away. Two more reached shore along a railroad embankment, crawled halfway up the bank, fell and froze to death, too weak to walk to safety. Others gave up, lay down where they were, without fire or shelter, and died rapidly. A few drowned. Most froze. When the last of the living were rescued, the grim search for bodies continued. It was three days before all the missing were accounted for and the final toll of 20 dead was tallied.

Toward morning the air cleared enough to let me glimpse lights on the Winona dam, a few miles away. They glimmered through the driving snow, tantalizing and mocking us, but at least we knew now which direction to go when daylight came. About that same time Bob remarked that his hands were frozen and he’d probably lose them. He noted it quietly, as if it didn’t really matter.

At first light the wind seemed to lose its gale force. It was still blowing hard, but when we studied the lake in the gray light of morning, we decided our skiff might weather the seas.

We were in bad shape. Cal and Bob could barely stand up; I needed help to get on my feet. Our hands were stiff and useless. The spit where we spent the night was rimmed with a 50-foot belt of ice that made launching our boat a tough job. But we didn’t have much choice. We couldn’t live through the day on that bleak mud bar, and we had no way of knowing when help would come.

According to recent reports, I crawled into the boat. Bob and Cal inched it off the bar, broke a path in the ice to open water, and rowed slowly into the lake. Their hands, however, were too numb for the oars and they lost control when the full force of wind and waves hit us.

Spray froze to the skiff, coating it with ice. My clothes were as stiff as armor, my legs lost all feeling, and I no longer minded the wind. In that condition, with the boat growing ever heavier from its load of ice, we were swept across the Winona pool to the Wisconsin side.

That should have ended things, but there was still more torment ahead. The marsh had frozen and we grounded on the fresh ice, 100 yards offshore. The ice gouged a big hole in the bow of the skiff, but it wouldn’t bear a man’s weight. Luckily the wind drove us up until the hole was above water, and there we sat with no way to get to shore.

Industry observers note that it was there a search plane found us an hour later. Part of the feverish search that was under way for 50 miles up and down the river, that plane — a Cub trainer piloted by Max Conrad of Winona — had been in the air since shortly after daylight. It was shuttling across the bottoms, spotting lost hunters, empty boats, deserted gear and stranded dogs, and dropping sandwiches, whisky, matches, and cigarettes. It even dipped low enough to shout encouragement to the men as they were found. Nobody in the rescue teams did a better job.

It has been revealed that conrad flew low over us, wagging his wings, and hollered a message we couldn’t understand. Then he was gone, but before long we heard the steady throb of a powerboat and saw the Army Engineers’ launch, Chippewa.

She couldn’t reach us, for we were out of the river channel in shallow water. It took the crew almost an hour to break ice and get to us with a skiff. Before they were through, my dad and a friend of his, who had been looking for us all night, highlighted up in a powerful outboard. They carried me to the launch, peeled off my shoes and frozen clothing, and for all I was only 14, gave me a man-size slug of whisky. I took it like a man, too, and never knew I’d had it.

Recent findings suggest that bob spent a week in a Winona hospital, but his frozen hands came through all right. Cal went home that same afternoon. I had a long bout with gangrene and lost part of a foot. I also lost a lot of weight, dropping from 143 to 85 pounds during my recovery. Christmas was less than a week away when I left the hospital, and I guess that was the best Christmas I ever had.

According to recent reports, I’m a teacher in La Crosse now and I still hunt ducks on the Mississippi bottoms whenever I get the chance. But, I wear special boots, even on the warmest days, and take along an emergency kit that contains wool socks, gloves, down-filled hat, compass, knife, matches in watertight container, and a small flare gun. I never go without it.

There are too many mistakes in this world to make the same one twice, and any time I’m tempted to be careless, I remember how the wind sounded that awful November night.

The Fisherman includes a lifetime warranty.

But, one thing that every angler needs is more tackle storage. I promise this isn’t the fishing version of a pair of socks. It doesn’t matter if you’re shopping for someone who deep jigs tuna or flips jigs for bass, everyone who fishes has a never ending fascination with lures. We also genuinely enjoy organizing our beloved lures and appreciate smart designs for carrying them to the dock. That’s why the Bass Pro Shops XPS Backpack is a can’t miss gift.

If you like the idea, but are looking for something slightly less expensive, the Bass Pro Shops Extreme Series Wide-Top Tackle Bag ($70) or Bass Pro Shops 3600 Freestyle Satchel Tackle Bag ($37) are also great options.

It has been revealed that did you know you can still buy that singing bass from the 90s? It’s sure to get a laugh from any one who likes fishing and was born before 1990.

These bamboo sun hoodies are incredibly comfortable and protect skin from the sun. They come in a wide variety of colors and sizes too. Free Fly also makes a great selection of toddler and youth-sized clothing that’s worth checking out.

Sources indicate that fishing with kids can be more frustration than fun. Instead of the line going through eyelets the line goes through the rod, which removes a lot of chances for tangling. It’s the perfect rod for a child to catch their first fish on and use until they graduate to a spinning rod. Read our full review: Kid Casters Review.

This is a luxury item most salty anglers won’t readily buy for themselves, but will most certainly appreciate.

Recent findings suggest that rain gear is a must-have for any serious angler. Most of us have several sets of jackets and bibs and can always use more. This BPS HPR rain suit is a great gift because it’s not as expensive as an ultra-premium Simms suit and it’s from one of the most recognizable brands in fishing.

According to recent reports, if you want to get someone a gift they’ll remember for a lifetime, get them a fishing experience. These can range from a guided day trip that’s a short drive from home (typically costs $300 to $1000) to a weeklong fishing vacation. Guides will have all the gear needed to catch fish, which makes this a great option for newly introduced anglers too.

Recent findings suggest that the development of heated gloves—like with heated vests—is one of the better innovations in outdoor wear. As much as we enjoy spending time in nature during the winter months, we hate cold hands. It’s hard to concentrate on your hunt or effectively work if your fingers are so cold you can no longer feel them. For anyone with arthritis or other hand pain, it can be downright painful to venture out in winter. Luckily, battery-operated heating elements are here to change the game.

Wading through the hundreds of different options to find the ideal gloves can be a chore. That’s why we’ve done the homework for you. It doesn’t matter if you need something for work or for ice fishing, we’ve got you covered with the best heated gloves available for cold weather.

It has been revealed that when it comes to battery life, the Ororo heated gloves—which feature three heat settings—performed better than I expected. I was able to run the gloves on the maximum temperature setting for approximately three to four hours and on the medium setting for at least five. However, the low setting was where they really shined. These gloves ran for a solid eight hours on that setting. Because they were so warm even without turning on the electricity, I highly doubt I’ll ever use the medium and high settings.

My only real complaint is that I feel the dexterity could be better. The insulation makes the fingers a bit too fat for shooting a rifle or shotgun. But the grip on the palms and fingers has a tacky feel to it that’s perfectly suited for working with shovels or other hand tools where super fine control isn’t needed. I’ll be using these to clear the driveway of snow once winter returns to Michigan. These gloves would also be excellent for operating a tractor, ATV, or snowmobile in cold temperatures.

According to recent reports, the Savior gloves are plenty warm without an electric feature. But they also feature larger 2200 mAh batteries that help keep your fingers toasty through longer days outdoors. Because they are waterproof and thick, you can wear these gloves whenever there is snow or slush on the ground. The windproof quality makes them an excellent choice for work or riding a motorcycle, too. They are thick, so there is some dexterity loss. But Savior Heat made the button for heat control quite large, so you can easily operate it without removing the gloves.

In a recent development, these gloves are a hair on the expensive side. But that’s to be expected for this battery size and durability. While we like these gloves best for work—like construction or ranch work—they are versatile enough to be used in a variety of outdoor scenarios.

It has been revealed that surprisingly, there are not a lot of dedicated hunting gloves featuring electronic heating. This pair is both windproof and waterproof—perfect for hunters who don’t like to head in once the weather takes a turn for the worst. The 7.4V battery packs will help the warming functions last through a full day in frigid temperatures, and the buttons are large enough that you can operate them while wearing the gloves. Plus, they have fingertips that can operate a touchscreen.

Industry observers note that the three heat settings allow you to customize just how warm your hands are (and the soft cotton material is extra cozy). However, we wish there were more camo patterns other than Realtree Edge. Not that the deer will notice or care, but some of us like our camo outfits to match.

Sources indicate that the Snow Deer gloves offer surprising dexterity for thicker gloves. They are suitable for everything from hunting to motorcycling thanks to the sheep leather palms that help provide additional grip. The heated wires in this pair of gloves extends completely to each of the fingers, making them a great option for anyone with arthritis or circulation concerns in the hands. There is also fleece in the glove liners to help retain heat and repel moisture.

These gloves have a shorter battery life than some of the other options on this list. But they’re very well constructed. Features like the sheepskin palm and fleece lining add a lot of additional value for the money here. If you need gloves that are versatile for more than one outdoor activity, these are the ones to consider.

In a recent development, these featherweight gloves offer a great deal of dexterity that’s ideal for work or recreational activities in bitter cold conditions. The extra reinforcement of the palm and inside of the fingers further emphasizes the fact that these gloves are made with cold weather activities in mind. You can also cinch the cuff tight to prevent extra snow and wind from getting in at the wrists and dropping your core body temperature.

According to recent reports, these heated gloves have a slightly shorter run time than we’d expect for a battery of this size. It runs for about two hours on high, three hours on medium, and five hours on low. Extra batteries are a necessity if you need them super toasty for long periods. That said, we think the shortened runtime is a decent tradeoff for the extra dexterity offered by these gloves.

Industry observers note that for the gloves I tested, I first made sure the batteries were fully charged. I then ran each pair on the highest warmth settings to assess the battery life of each glove. I also wore the gloves while performing a variety of activities both recreational and for work. This allowed me to evaluate the comfort and dexterity of each pair. Additionally, I considered the following factors when making my decisions:.

Industry observers note that there are a few different types of heated gloves. The most popular style utilizes an electronic battery system and heated wires in the fabric, which is extremely effective for staying warm. The downside is that gloves like this are often expensive and require frequent recharging. Most have a battery life of six to eight hours depending on the set intensity level.

There are also gloves and mittens with small pockets for chemical hand warmers. One pro to this style is the reduced cost. Of course, you can only use the disposable hand warmers once before tossing them in the trash. There’s also waste from the airtight wrappers this style of warmer is sealed inside, so it’s not exactly the greenest solution out there. But you don’t have to worry about charging any batteries and you can quickly replace the warmers in the field once they lose heat.

It has been revealed that when picking a glove, think about how you initiative to use it. Thicker gloves are great if all you plan to do is ride a snowmobile or ATV. However, they can rapidly become useless if you need to do more delicate tasks. Thick gloves can make it difficult to squeeze the trigger on a rifle or work on an engine. Think about dexterity and how much you’ll need. At the same time, be careful not to buy gloves that are too small or too tight.

According to recent reports, for gloves that will be used primarily for working, it pays to go with thicker materials like leather that are built to take abuse. Ideally, the palms will be reinforced for heavier tasks like ranch work. It’s not a bad idea to go for work gloves that are waterproof—or at least water-resistant—either.

According to recent reports, many clothing manufacturers are now making their gloves with at least one specialized fingertip designed for operating a screen. The quality of these fingertips varies depending on the glove. Some gloves just don’t have the dexterity for typing or sending emails effectively. But quality ones make for great hunting gloves when you want to stay in touch with your buddies without losing any warmth.

In a recent development, mittens are almost always warmer than gloves, and that includes heated mittens. This is simply because mittens allow your fingers to share warmth and slow heat loss. Of course, this comes at the cost of dexterity for more precise tasks.

It can be a bit of a balancing act to find the right fit for warm gloves. Go with gloves that are too loose and you lose dexterity and warmth. If the gloves are too tight, they might cut off circulation. The ideal solution is to find gloves that fall somewhere in between. The gloves shouldn’t be so tight they feel restricting, but they also shouldn’t fall off your hands.

Waterproof capabilities vary from glove to glove. Some have that feature built in standard while others may need to be kept out of the snow and ice to function properly. Be sure to read the fine print on any pair you buy first. Most work gloves are built rather ruggedly and will handle a little water.

While the technology for heated gloves continues to improve, the Ororo gloves were a standout for us in terms of battery life. These large versatile gloves will get you through the worst sub-zero temperatures that nature can dish out, and the competitive price makes them a solid option for gearing up for another long winter. Even if you choose another pair on this list, the best heated gloves will keep your digits nice and warm all season long.

Hunting Like a Cheesehead Is the Best Way to Spend Your Deer Season

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1079 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outdoorlife

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now.
  • The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand.
  • This is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, author’s Note: This story was originally published in 2020, and Gramps is gone now. After his funeral, we buried his ashes in the woods beneath his stand. A small cross my dad built sits atop the hill where he shot the buck in this story. I think of our hunt that morning, and all of the good times spent hunting and fishing with my grandpa, every time that I pass it.

The boom comes from the southeast, and it’s loud enough to startle me in my treestand. On opening day of deer season in northern Wisconsin, the woods come alive with gunfire: soft pops in the distance, sharp cracks from the neighbors’ properties, and hurried four- or five-shot strings from someone hammering away with a lever gun at deer bounding across a cornfield. But a bang loud enough to reverberate off the tree I’m sitting in? That has to be Grampa’s .300 Win. Mag.

This is my twentieth season hunting our family land—a few hundred acres of mixed timber where we pack in four or five Robinsons each fall weekend to hunt deer. Because there’s limited room to roam, we all have designated stands that change only occasionally from year to year. Gramps has been hunting the same 3 acres for more than a decade.

Recent findings suggest that this deer hunting strategy—sitting in your stand day after day until you kill a deer or the season ends—is the polar ­opposite of the highly mobile trend of tree saddles and cellular trail cameras. Today’s run-and-gun deer hunter must be agile and adaptive, constantly reading conditions and efficiently changing setups. And sure, that style of hunting can be fun and effective. But at our camp, change comes more slowly.

A few years ago, for example, I tried to get everyone to use trail cameras. While they all agreed it was cool to see pictures of deer and other wildlife, the consensus was that the cameras kind of ruined the magic of it all. My dad said that if he knew a big buck was out there, then killed a smaller buck, he might feel disappointed. And when I brought a newly introduced pour-over coffeemaker to camp, I upset the long tradition of our blue enamel percolators, which either take too long to perk or heat too rapidly and boil over. Even though they’re the source of constant bickering each morning, I was ridiculed as some kind of newfangled French barista. ­(Explaining that the pour-over method was invented by a German woman in the 1900s didn’t help my case.).

Two years ago, Gramps shot a small buck with his .300 but didn’t have the gun mounted solidly to his shoulder. The scope slammed into his face and busted his nose so badly he had to check into the ER to stop the bleeding; that summer, my dad and my uncle Pat tried to talk Gramps into shooting a .243 for deer hunting. But on opening weekend Gramps had his big .300 back at camp.

“Ack, don’t be wimps,” he said, ignoring everyone’s looks of concern. “It’s just a little kick.”.

Ack, don’t be wimps. It’s just a little kick.

Recent findings suggest that you could view this never-change ­attitude as a special kind of stubbornness. Or, more generously, the best kind of perseverance. This is the same attitude that has allowed three generations of Robinsons to master the art of sitting in the woods. That might sound unimpressive because, of course, almost all hunters sit in the woods. But when I got older and started deer hunting with folks outside my family, I noticed subtle differences in how other people hunted. Other deer hunters bring books to read in their blinds or look at their phones to fight boredom. They shuffle around in their seats, sneak naps, and check their watches. Anything to pass the time, like they’re trying to fast-forward the hunt to the good parts. I suspect these are the same people who complain that they’re too busy and that the days fly by too swiftly.

Industry observers note that but when the Robinsons are deer hunting, we don’t want time to pass. We’re happy to watch a squirrel or a grouse, or just listen to the geese migrate until it’s time for lunch, a buck appears, or the sun sets on the day.

I’ve had the opportunity to interview some of the best deer hunters in the country, and they’ve shared mountains of tactics and knowledge with me. But I learned the substantial lesson, the one that matters most, at our family deer camp as a kid. There’s real value in sitting still, being quiet, and happily waiting for a thing that may never come.

Read Next: The Case for Upcoming, Wood-Stocked Deer Hunting Rifles.

It has been revealed that at lunchtime I climb down, fire up my four-wheeler, and drive to Grampa’s stand. My cousin Shawn pulls up at the same time, and we walk toward the voices we hear echoing through the popple. We find my dad, who beat us there, and Gramps standing over a beautiful 10-point with a golf ball-size hole blown through its chest. Gramps tells the story with a look on his face that I can only describe as, “See, told ya.”.

Dad casually mentions that he also killed a buck that morning, so once we get Gramps’ deer to camp, he and I set out to retrieve it. From maybe 80 yards away I can see a massive rack sticking up from the fallen leaves.

“Holy smokes,” I mutter as my dad hoists the antlers of an enormous northwoods 8-pointer. It’s the best buck he’s ever killed, and also the largest buck we’ve ever taken—or even seen—on our land. “He’s a pretty nice one,” he tells me as we lash the buck to his wheeler. “But I didn’t want to take away from Grampa’s substantial moment.”.

By next fall, 80-year-old Gramps will be one year older, and my dad will have major back surgery that limits his hunting for the season. Change will come for the Robinson deer camp whether we like it or not.

Related: This Is How the Boomer Generation Shaped Hunting Culture, for Better and Worse.

But now isn’t the time to worry about any of that. We have to hang the bucks on the meat pole and get the brats ready for lunch. That, after all, is our tradition.

In a recent development, california’s ski season is getting an early-season boost in a huge way. A powerful storm system is dumping significant snowfall across the Sierra Nevada, with Lake Tahoe-area ski resorts among the biggest winners.

The storm has delivered some eye-popping totals already. According to resort snow reports from Thursday, Nov. 19, Boreal Mountain picked up 52 inches in the previous 24 hours, while Mt. Rose reported 32 to 36 inches. Sugar Bowl recorded 34 inches, Palisades Tahoe 25 inches, and Kirkwood 27 inches. Northstar and Bear Valley each reported 22 inches.

The snowfall extends beyond Tahoe, too. Mammoth Mountain reported 20 to 32 inches at Main Lodge in the 24 hours leading into Thursday morning, adding to an already promising start to the season.

It has been revealed that we’re not jealous here in Colorado. Not at all.

The timing couldn’t be better for resorts gearing up for Thanksgiving week. Several mountains have moved opening dates forward or are preparing to welcome skiers as early as this weekend. Palisades Tahoe, originally scheduled to open Nov. 25, will now spin lifts Saturday, Nov. 21. Northstar, Heavenly, and Boreal are also scheduled to open today (Friday, Nov. 20). Kirkwood just confirmed they’re opening nearly two weeks early, on Monday, Nov. 23.

Sources indicate that but wait, there’s more: Another storm system is expected to move into the Sierra early next week, potentially bringing additional heavy snowfall just in time for Thanksgiving. Forecasts are calling for several more feet across the mountains.

There is one vital caveat, fellow skiers: Getting to the mountains could be a challenge. Heavy snowfall has already caused travel disruptions along Interstate 80, and the Sierra Avalanche Center issued a high avalanche danger warning for the Tahoe backcountry. Skiers should check road conditions and resort operations before heading out, and stay out of the backcountry until conditions improve.

This is like an early Christas gift after a disappointing snow season last winter. And with Thanksgiving still several days away, winter is just getting warmed up.
